articles.title: North Korea Wants Security Talks With the US, Not Nuclear Talks
articles.body:
Since the start of his second administration, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly proposed renewed talks with North Korea. Pyongyang has said that relations could improve if Washington respected its nuclear status and abandoned what it calls its “hostile policy.” But what would North Korea be willing to talk about if discussions resumed?
Pyongyang increasingly seeks talks on its security concerns, particularly U.S. military policy and the regional security environment, while treating its own possession of nuclear weapons as non-negotiable. It may even demand a halt to U.S. military exercises with its allies as a precondition for talks.
What Pyongyang Learned From Hanoi
The failure of the 2019 North Korea-Trump summit in Hanoi may have prompted Pyongyang to reassess its negotiating strategy and strengthen its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons. At the summit, North Korea sought partial relief from United Nations sanctions in exchange for dismantling its Yongbyon nuclear facilities. Washington, however, sought denuclearization measures extending beyond Yongbyon in exchange for a broader package of economic benefits. The summit ended without an agreement.
Why did North Korea not accept Washington’s “big deal”? Shortly after the summit collapsed, North Korean Foreign Minister Ri Yong Ho explained that security guarantees mattered more to Pyongyang than sanctions relief. North Korea had nevertheless proposed partial sanctions relief in return for dismantling Yongbyon because it believed Washington would find it difficult to take military measures at the time.
North Korea may have recognized the limits of what the United States could offer in terms of security guarantees. U.S. military strategy in Northeast Asia is not solely a response to the North Korean threat. It also reflects Washington’s alliance commitments to South Korea and Japan and its broader strategic competition with China. Even if North Korea gave up all its nuclear weapons, Washington might not be able to offer the security guarantees Pyongyang wants, given its regional interests and alliance commitments. From this perspective, North Korea’s attempt in Hanoi to exchange partial denuclearization for partial sanctions relief may have been a realistic approach. The failure in Hanoi appears to have convinced Pyongyang that giving up its nuclear weapons would not secure the guarantees it sought. After Hanoi, North Korea reinforced its commitment to retaining nuclear weapons through legislation and constitutional changes. In September 2022, it adopted a new law on nuclear forces policy. Kim Jong Un declared that North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state was irreversible and ruled out further negotiations on giving up its nuclear weapons or on denuclearization.
North Korea did not begin identifying itself as a nuclear weapon state in 2022. It had already codified that status in a 2013 law “consolidating the position of nuclear weapons state for self-defense.” Article 9 of that law, however, expressed support for international nuclear disarmament efforts. The omission of that provision from the 2022 law was therefore significant.
The 2022 law not only entrenched nuclear possession as a permanent foundation of national strategy but also called for qualitative and quantitative improvements in nuclear forces in response to external threats and changes in the international nuclear balance. In this context, a freeze on nuclear weapons production or a reduction in its nuclear arsenal could conflict with this policy if North Korea’s security environment remained unchanged.
Setting the Terms for Renewed Talks
North Korea’s recent statements on relations with Washington indicate that it expects changes in U.S. policy before talks resume, while treating its nuclear possession as non-negotiable.
In October 2025, Trump publicly expressed his desire to meet Kim Jong Un again during his trip to Asia. That didn’t eventuate, but Trump is reportedly looking at the possibility of a meeting with Kim during his next trip to Asia in November 2026.
At the Ninth Workers’ Party Congress in February 2026, Kim Jong Un stated that relations with the United States could improve if Washington respected North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapon state and abandoned its hostile policy. He thus linked improved relations to a change in Washington’s attitude toward a nuclear-armed North Korea and its policy toward Pyongyang.
In August, Trump again expressed interest in meeting Kim and ordered a reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises. Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un’s sister and an authoritative voice for the regime, dismissed the move as insufficient. She argued that holding the exercises at all demonstrated Washington’s hostility. Kim Yo Jong’s response suggested that Pyongyang wanted the exercises halted altogether, rather than merely scaled back, before agreeing to talks. In the same statement, she also criticized South Korea’s push to acquire nuclear-powered submarines.
In September, Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui reaffirmed that North Korea’s nuclear status was irreversible. She rejected the coexistence of confrontation and dialogue in relations with North Korea and argued that a geopolitical realignment centered on a nuclear-armed North Korea was inevitable. Her statement reinforced the message that Washington could not maintain policies Pyongyang regarded as hostile and expect dialogue to follow.
North Korea has long sought security guarantees and an end to Washington’s hostile policy. The difference now is that Pyongyang treats its nuclear possession as non-negotiable and expects changes in U.S. attitudes and military policy before talks resume. A reduction in South Korea-U.S. military exercises alone appears insufficient to meet its demands. Its criticism of South Korea’s nuclear-powered submarine plans also suggests concern about potential U.S. support for such capabilities.
This departs from the Singapore agreement, which paired a commitment to denuclearization with improved relations and the establishment of a peace regime. Pyongyang now seeks U.S. policy changes as the starting point for diplomacy, rather than as part of a bargain over giving up its nuclear weapons.
North Korea’s strategy notwithstanding, its ability to change U.S. policy is not guaranteed. Despite Trump’s efforts to engage Pyongyang, the United States, South Korea, and Japan continue to reaffirm the goal of North Korea’s denuclearization, while Washington maintains its defense commitments to its allies.
Pyongyang may see no need to rush into talks. It continues to build up its nuclear forces, citing security threats, while strengthening ties with its partners.
In September 2026, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported signs of a new uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon and indications of expanded operations at Kangson. North Korea has also recently increased the frequency of its missile tests. Meanwhile, expanding military cooperation with Russia and improving relations with China are giving Pyongyang greater room to resist international pressure, including sanctions. Both countries oppose further sanctions on North Korea and have become quieter on its denuclearization.
North Korea may believe that time is on its side: As its nuclear capabilities grow and its diplomatic options expand, Washington may eventually have no choice but to enter talks on the basis that North Korea will retain its nuclear weapons.
How the United States Should Respond
Washington’s first task is to clarify the conditions under which North Korea is willing to negotiate and the agenda it is prepared to discuss. Some experts argue that a nuclear freeze or reductions should serve as interim goals if complete denuclearization cannot be achieved in the short term. This may be a realistic alternative for the United States, but Washington should not assume that Pyongyang will accept it as a topic for negotiation. North Korea may instead demand that negotiations focus on regional security issues or insist on changes in U.S. policy before agreeing to talks.
To clarify these issues, working-level meetings should precede any new North Korea-U.S. summit. Washington must coordinate closely with Seoul and Tokyo before negotiating measures that affect their security. If Pyongyang raises concerns about U.S. military activities on the Korean Peninsula, Washington should assess whether its demands can be addressed through reciprocal military measures.
Discussing regional security does not necessarily mean recognizing North Korea as a nuclear-weapon state or weakening allied military readiness. With South Korea’s agreement, for example, the United States could consider adjusting the scale or format of joint exercises in exchange for limits on North Korean exercises in specific areas, with arrangements for both sides to verify compliance. Once military crisis-management measures are in place and the security environment improves, Washington could argue that Pyongyang should move toward a nuclear freeze or reductions.
The United States must also challenge North Korea’s calculation that time is on its side. Maintaining existing sanctions and deterrence alone is unlikely to change Pyongyang’s strategic judgment. The United States should make clear that North Korea’s continued nuclear buildup could lead South Korea and Japan to strengthen their military capabilities and fuel calls in both countries for nuclear weapons of their own. An offer to discuss regional security should accompany that message. The aim should be to create incentives for diplomacy without triggering another arms race.
Washington should use security talks to pursue reciprocal military measures and build a path toward limits on North Korea’s nuclear capabilities. Knowing what each side is willing to offer before the next summit would improve the chances of reaching an agreement.

articles.title: Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy
After 20 months of upheaval in transatlantic relations, EU officials fear the U.S. president dislikes Ukraine’s leader too much to push for a fair peace.
U.S. President Donald Trump with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images
In a throwaway comment this week, Donald Trump made clear that he does not regard the war in Ukraine as a conflict with fault on both sides. “Russia frankly has been fine on Ukraine,” the U.S. president said. “They have not been doing that much.”
To residents of Kyiv — who have endured weeks of intensifying bombardment — and Ukraine’s allies across Europe, the remark confirmed a growing impression that the U.S. is taking Russia leader Vladimir Putin’s side in the war.
“American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years,” the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday. The reason Ukraine hasn’t “surrendered on Putin’s terms” so far is because Europe has been providing so much support, she added.

As they scratch their heads for explanations for Trump’s latest turn against Ukraine, some European officials and diplomats think it comes down to the president’s personal preferences, as much as his country’s political aims.
“I do think it’s a personal thing,” said former British Cabinet minister David Lidington, now distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a leading security think tank in London. “Trump is self-centered — his personal predilections for dictators and autocrats, his desire to give opportunities to U.S. businesses … are very important parts of his motivation.”
In private, EU officials agree. “Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. He just doesn’t like him,” said one government official who has observed both men closely. “That makes it harder to get the U.S. to help on peace. Everything is a rational business deal with Trump, until it’s not.”
A diplomat from an EU country — granted anonymity, like others in this report, to discuss sensitive matters — said the inconsistent Trump could change his mind again and reverse recent moves against Ukraine. The U.S. president has chopped and changed on many issues, “except one thing,” the diplomat said. “He seems to be supportive of the Russians.”
“He’s been critical of Ukraine, the EU, NATO, but hardly ever said anything critical about Putin. It is striking. We have to deal with an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else,” the diplomat said.
The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

After four-and-a-half years of war, Kyiv is running low on funding, air defenses and — amid swelling support for Europe’s populist right — facing a potential loss of political support in the months ahead.
Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff met the Ukrainian president and the leaders of Norway and Finland for talks in Oslo on Tuesday, and will head to St. Petersburg to discuss peace proposals with the Russian leadership on Wednesday as the White House pushes hard for a ceasefire. One option Putin will be offered is a three-way leaders’ summit with Trump and Zelenskyy.
Previous efforts to get the Russian president to attend such a meeting have failed, however, and EU diplomats do not believe Putin is showing any genuine desire for a ceasefire. That is partly what makes Trump’s hostility toward Zelenskyy so problematic.
“There is a clear consensus across Europe that Putin does not want peace,” a second EU diplomat said. “He will need to be forced into peace.”

But instead of making demands of Putin, Trump has ratcheted up his pressure on Zelenskyy, even amid escalating Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities this month. Ukraine’s leader is feeling the strain, as he told his EU counterparts in private meetings in Brussels last week, according to the first diplomat.
In a succession of highly critical comments in recent days, Trump has said Zelenskyy “doesn’t care” and “doesn’t want to end this war;” and should be replaced as leader or as Ukraine’s negotiator. “President Putin would like to see a settlement,” Trump said. “President Zelenskyy could have solved this war, or he could have made a deal, many times.”

The Oval Office beating
Trump’s animosity may date back to an incident during his first term in 2019, when he urged the Ukrainian leader to help with an investigation into Joe Biden, who eventually defeated Trump in the following presidential election, Lidington said. A succession of hostile encounters in the years since — including in the Oval Office in February 2025 — have reinforced the impression, he said.
“It was clear that in the infamous meeting in the White House that Trump and [Vice President JD] Vance had planned that public beating-up of Zelenskyy and it struck me then that there was a strong personal element to this,” said Lidington.
“I think there’s another element, which is that if you look at the people Trump tries to court, it tends to be autocratic strongman — and it is ‘man’ — leaders,” Lidington said.
He recalled attending a dinner with world leaders in 2018 to mark the centenary of the end of World War I in Paris. French President Emmanuel Macron and the German chancellor at the time, Angela Merkel, were playing joint hosts “at the top table,” but Trump was not interested in making small talk with either of them, Lidington said.
“It was pretty obvious from the body language that Trump was impatient with them and one of the people he really wanted to talk to was [Turkish leader Recep Tayyip] Erdoğan and other people who were a bit more in that strongman image that he likes to portray himself,” he observed.
‘Strange stories’
A senior official from a European country familiar with the Ukraine talks said Trump’s motives were partly political, partly about calculating what would be profitable and partly about personalities.

“They are currently in an election cycle and need someone to blame for rising prices,” the official said. “In general, Trump tends to like various types of people and leaders. He actually has a fondness for successful and cheerful people.”
In recent days, Zelenskyy has warned his country is suffering more civilian casualties because the U.S. has cut back on support, including Starlink and Starshield services that help Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks and plan operations. “We still have no explanation for this, just different strange stories,” Zelenskyy told U.S. congressmen on Monday.
This month, the advanced warnings of incoming Russian missile attacks from U.S. partners have failed to come through as normal. Ukraine is also running low on Patriot missile interceptors, he said.

Tuesday’s meeting with Witkoff in Norway raised the possibility that direct engagement with Putin might be back on the cards, for Zelenskyy at least.

The process is now going in the right direction again, he added. “Hopefully, we don’t do any backtracking.”

Kyiv • UNN
Russia has intensified its drone attacks, seeking to exhaust air defenses and pressure Ukraine. Stronger defense and strikes against Russia's military-industrial complex could reduce the attacks.
Russia continues its massive drone attacks on Ukraine and is attempting to cover as large an area as possible with its strikes. Military expert Oleh Zhdanov told a UNN journalist more about why the Russian Federation is relying on massive air attacks, how they are connected to political pressure on Ukraine, and what could force Russia to reduce the intensity of its strikes.
Details
Russian drone attacks are taking place virtually around the clock, but the nature of the air strikes changed at the end of October. According to the military expert, whereas reactive drones predominated earlier, Russia is now once again actively using conventional attack drones. In addition, the enemy is attempting to simultaneously cover as much of Ukrainian territory as possible with its attacks.
It is very strange that now "our old song is starting again—we are starting it all over again." In the sense that they are now going to attack 24/7. And what have they been doing all this time? Even now, if you look out the window, air raid alerts are in effect 24/7 across most of Ukraine. And we made it through the whole of September like that
Russia plans to increase drone production: Politico learned the details21.09.26, 10:29 • 5874 views
At the same time, Oleh Zhdanov noted that at the end of September, short intervals began to appear between drone raids. In particular, in Kyiv and other cities, there was sometimes approximately an hour between successive attacks, but at the end of October, Russia once again intensified its attacks.
The difference at the end of October is that they began trying to cover all of Ukraine. They have returned again: whereas in September they were mostly reactive, now they have once again added conventional "Shaheds" and "Geran-2" drones. And their number is greater—more than half of the drones in these continuous raids at present
Ballistic missiles also remain a separate threat; their launches, Oleh Zhdanov emphasizes, are more difficult to predict. He explains that recently Russia has used them at intervals of approximately once every 7–10 days. Moreover, the intensity of such strikes may vary, so Ukraine must also be prepared for combined attacks.
Will Russia have enough resources for continuous attacks
The expert notes that Russia is using the means of destruction at its disposal, while the scale of drone use depends, in particular, on production capabilities.
They can provide a large number of drones—and they do. Note that in September they were stockpiling conventional "Geran-2" drones. In fact, they used very few of them for a month, and then in the first ten days of October they carried out two powerful strikes, when the number of conventional drones exceeded 500 units. And now they are launching them within the limits produced by their enterprises
At the same time, Oleh Zhdanov believes that Russia has limited capacity to accumulate large stockpiles of weapons, so it is forced to constantly replenish the resources it has used. However, this does not mean that the intensity of the attacks will necessarily decrease in the near future.
They are essentially operating straight from the production line; there are very few stockpiles at present. And I say again, we have two options: the first is to destroy their production facilities, but we cannot reach them, plus they have now begun burying the same "Geran" drones in the ground. So the second option is to build an air defense system in a new, modern sense, rather than according to the old approaches of the Soviet Union or the Second World War
Why Russia is relying on drones
Massive drone attacks allow Russia to exhaust Ukrainian air defenses over a prolonged period and create a constant threat to the civilian population and infrastructure. In the expert's view, the Kremlin seeks to use these strikes as an instrument of pressure on Ukrainians in order to secure concessions on its own terms.
The objective is one and only one—to break public opinion so that people agree to capitulate on the terms of the Russian Federation. And now, by the way, negotiations are underway in Norway, and it is the same old song: "Surrender, and everything will be fine for you. If you do not surrender to us, we will continue the shelling." That's all
The expert also links the intensity of Russian attacks, in particular, to the upcoming midterm elections in the United States and negotiations on ending the war, in order to increase pressure on Ukraine precisely during periods of important international events.
Absolutely. putin always ties powerful shelling of Ukraine and massive combined strikes to political events. Today, the midterm elections in the United States are at the top of our agenda. And in fact, in my view, both Trump and putin have simultaneously gone all in. They are applying pressure in every way they can, - with all available forces and means
What could force Russia to reduce the number of strikes
The expert identifies strengthening Ukraine’s air defense as one of the key areas for countering Russian attacks. In his opinion, it is necessary to improve the ability to intercept targets at short and medium ranges, as well as to develop weapons capable of destroying threats before they are used. In addition, strikes against Russia’s military-industrial enterprises also play an important role.
Sanctions are a long song. And the most effective sanctions are our missiles and our drones. Unfortunately, our strikes against military-industrial complex enterprises are not as powerful as one would like, because even a drone carrying 100 kilograms of explosives is not a missile carrying 300 or 500 kilograms of explosives
Oleh Zhdanov also drew attention to the importance of ballistic weapons, which, according to him, could enhance Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian launchers and other military targets. At the same time, the effectiveness of countermeasures depends not only on the availability of such weapons, but also on the ability to detect targets in a timely manner and strike them. The expert believes that the development of indigenous missile technologies could become one of the factors deterring Russian attacks.
If we had ballistic missiles, we would take out the launchers or at least drive them away from the border so that they could not reach our territory. There is very little time to hit a launcher at its launch position or in the loading area. That is why Russia is very afraid of Ukraine acquiring ballistic weapons

articles.title: Hegseth and Netanyahu hold secret talks – Axios
articles.body:
Hegseth and Netanyahu hold secret talks – Axios
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has made an unannounced visit to Israel for talks with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu just days before the country’s parliamentary elections, according to Axios.
The reported meeting comes as Washington and Israel discuss potentially resuming major military operations against Iran, while indirect negotiations continue over the war they launched in February. Israel, a major recipient of American military funding and weapons, has justified its offensives on security grounds, even as the conflict has spread across the region, disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and driven up global energy prices.
Hegseth met Netanyahu on Monday at Ovda Air Base in southern Israel, where US fighter jets and refueling aircraft are stationed, Axios reported on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the visit. The Pentagon chief also met American troops deployed at the facility.
The talks were held behind closed doors, with neither side publicly disclosing what was discussed, the outlet said. The Pentagon declined to comment on the meeting, while Hegseth acknowledged visiting US troops operating under Central Command.
The surprise visit followed US President Donald Trump’s public endorsement of Netanyahu ahead of the October 27 parliamentary elections – Israel’s first since the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks and the subsequent devastating Israeli military campaign in Gaza. On Sunday, the US president hailed Netanyahu as a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” and offered him his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”
“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump declared on Truth Social, praising the Israeli leader’s role in the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Netanyahu has ruled Israel for more than 18 years across several terms, longer than any other prime minister in the country’s history. He now faces a fierce battle to stay in power, with opponents blaming him for the catastrophic security failures of the October 7 attack and accusing him of prolonging the devastating war in Gaza to preserve his political survival. Polls suggest his right-wing coalition could lose its parliamentary majority.
Hegseth’s trip also reportedly comes as Washington and West Jerusalem discuss the possibility of unleashing another major military campaign against Iran. Trump has raised the prospect of renewed strikes after the US midterm elections in November.
Netanyahu has meanwhile made clear that Israel is prepared to attack Iran without waiting for Washington’s approval or participation.
“If we need to act alone, we will act alone,” he declared on Sunday, outlining a security doctrine centered on preemptive military action.
Netanyahu has also called for the overthrow of Iran’s government, claiming Tehran would continue to rebuild its military and nuclear capabilities as long as its current leadership remains in power. Iran has repeatedly denied seeking nuclear weapons, insisting its nuclear program is peaceful.

articles.title: Republicans Threaten to Block $350 Billion in Pentagon Funding Unless Trump Ramps Up Pressure on Russia
articles.body:
Some Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives are prepared to block additional Pentagon funding unless Donald Trump’s administration increases pressure on Russia.
The Hill reported on this.
The White House is seeking approval for at least $350 billion in new military spending after the November elections, before the current Congress’ term comes to an end.
Ukraine’s supporters among the president’s fellow Republicans oppose a deal with Vladimir Putin on importing Russian diesel fuel and restrictions on the use of the Starshield military satellite system by Ukrainian forces.
They are calling for sanctions pressure on Moscow to be reinstated and the restrictions to be lifted.
Congressman Don Bacon warned that, without a change in course, Congress would not support Trump’s legislative initiatives for the remainder of his term.
“Agencies will not receive funding if they do not do their jobs,” said Republican Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick.
The funding package championed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth includes, among other provisions, $17 billion for the Golden Dome missile defense system and $47 billion to expand ammunition production.
According to the media, Republican leaders will need the support of nearly all their party members in the House of Representatives to pass the package.
Militarnyi previously reported, citing Reuters, that the order to restrict Starshield operations in Ukraine came directly from the White House.
Its implementation coincided with Washington’s pressure on Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
On October 19, Volodymyr Zelensky stated that communication problems on the front lines persisted: in various sectors, equipment stopped working at speeds of 130–161 km/h. According to the President, this complicates logistics and drone use, particularly for jet-powered interceptor drones.

articles.title: Trump may completely halt the supply of Patriot missiles to Ukraine – NATO warns of the risks
articles.body:
Trump may completely halt the supply of Patriot missiles to Ukraine – NATO warns of the risks
Kyiv • UNN
NATO fears a complete halt to U.S. arms deliveries to Ukraine due to tensions between Zelenskyy and Trump. Patriot deliveries are already being delayed.
NATO representatives warned Ukrainian officials about the risk of a complete halt to the supply of U.S. weapons, including missiles for Patriot systems, due to deteriorating relations between Presidents Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump. Bloomberg reports this, citing informed sources, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the Alliance's leadership fears that relations between Kyiv and Washington could deteriorate completely. NATO representatives are urging the Ukrainian side to reduce tensions in its communication with the Trump administration in order to avoid further restrictions on military aid.
The PURL program, under which European countries purchase U.S. weapons for Ukraine, is a particular concern. The United States currently supplies only about 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, four times fewer than during Joe Biden's presidency.
U.S. delaying deliveries of missiles already paid for by European allies
Zelenskyy previously stated that U.S. missiles were arriving irregularly, despite European partners having already paid for the corresponding deliveries. In addition, according to him, the Pentagon failed several times to warn Ukraine about Russian missile attacks.
The situation is complicated by limited stocks of U.S. interceptors. According to Mark Cancian, an expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, the United States has approximately 800 Patriot missiles. At the same time, the Pentagon seeks to preserve reserves for operations in the Middle East and a potential conflict with China.
As The Washington Post previously reported, Washington is also delaying approval of the transfer of Patriot missiles to Ukraine from European countries. According to the publication's sources, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has neither approved nor rejected the relevant requests, leaving them without a final decision.

articles.title: Rubio said that the United States must weigh Ukraine’s need for air defense missiles against that of others
articles.body:
Rubio said that the United States must weigh Ukraine’s need for air defense missiles against that of others
Kyiv • UNN
The United States must balance the requests of Ukraine, other allies, and its own needs for interceptor missiles. Rubio assured that supplies are being replenished.
The United States must balance Ukraine’s urgent requests for air-defense missiles with similar demands from other allies, as well as the needs of its own military. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this on Tuesday, October 20, UNN reports, citing Bloomberg.
Details
The United States is responding to many such requests and cannot meet them all, Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday.
"I know that one of the things President Zelenskyy has talked about is that he has been trying to purchase interceptor missiles, and I understand that. So is every other country in the world," the U.S. secretary of state said.
He named Saudi Arabia and Israel among the other countries seeking to obtain these weapons and added: "We also have our own needs."
Rubio said he had spoken for about 45 minutes earlier on Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who, the publication writes, "is embroiled in an escalating dispute with Donald Trump." The U.S. president repeated his criticism on Monday following reports, according to the publication, from officials in Kyiv about restrictions on intelligence sharing.
Rubio said that the U.S. president had never ordered such changes and was upset by reports that were "inaccurate." Referring to reports that some Russian missiles had managed to strike Ukraine without the warnings they usually receive through U.S. intelligence, he said this could have resulted from a technical problem rather than a U.S. directive, the publication writes.
The U.S. secretary of state also sought to play down concerns expressed by some analysts that the United States currently has limited weapons stocks due to the cumulative effect of the war with Iran and the dispatch of a significant amount of weapons to Ukraine earlier, the publication notes.
"I think we are very satisfied with our stocks of various munitions, including interceptors," he said, adding that production had been increased.
"But it takes time to build up these stocks," Rubio emphasized.

articles.title: Is a Russian drone near you right now? Ukrainians have developed maps that track drones in near real time
articles.body:
Ukrainians can now check a free live map of where Russian attack targets are flying, a Ukrainian air-threat monitoring project called monitor announced on X on 13 October. The beta pulls public reports of drones in flight into a single view and lays them over official air raid alerts.
Russia now flies jet-powered drones, and some switch off their engines before an attack and glide in. Over a hundred drones can arrive in one night. Yet since September, drone-only yellow alerts in some Oblasts no longer shut everything down. So during drone alerts, some Ukrainians now stay at their desks rather than in shelters. The new maps offers them a quick look at the sky from a phone, even on a weak signal.
What the map shows
The launch post described the service as one that tries to show where each target is, using open sources and algorithmic processing. It said the beta focuses on drones, with other targets to follow.
The drone data does not come from radar. The service draws on regional Telegram channels that post where drones and missiles are flying over their own oblasts. It cross-checks those posts to estimate what each target is, roughly where it is, and where it is heading, the project explains. The same page already lists cruise and ballistic missiles among the targets. It also says the map is free, ad-free, and needs no registration, and that it runs in a browser or on Telegram, designed to work on a phone with a weak signal.
A target log lists each drone’s district and course. Alert data comes from alerts.in.ua, and areas under alert turn red or yellow. The map refreshes about every 20 seconds while targets are airborne.
However, the developers warn that the dots are only estimates and show up late. Some targets slip through untracked. That is why “an empty map does not mean you are safe,” they wrote. When sirens sound, they urge people to rely on official signals and take shelter.
On 17 October, the Defense Ministry said that Ukraine’s Air Alert app now maps the approximate position and heading of some targets. These include cruise missiles, Banderol drone-launched missiles, and Shahed-type drones. The data comes straight from the Air Force over secure channels.
For security reasons, it carries no exact coordinates or real-time tracking and may lag. Ballistic missiles and anything faster than 2,000 km/h don’t appear at all. The ministry’s advice matches monitor’s: get to a shelter first, then check the map from there.

articles.title: A diesel tank burns at Transneft’s Druzhba hub as Ukraine keeps striking Russian energy despite Trump’s pressure
articles.body:
Drones attacked an oil and fuel pumping station of Russia’s Druzhba pipeline system in Tambov Oblast overnight on 20 October, setting a diesel tank on fire, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported, citing locals. Druzhba, Russian for “friendship,” is a Soviet-era oil pipeline, about 4,000 km long, that carries Russian crude west to Europe, including through a branch that crosses Ukraine. The struck station is on its Russian section. Tambov Oblast Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov confirmed a fire at an unnamed enterprise in Michurinsk district after what he called a Ukrainian drone attack. The station lies about 400 km from the front line.
Ukraine has spent months striking the refineries, terminals, and pipelines that fund Russia’s war, and its Defense Ministry says the strikes have knocked out more than half of Russia’s refining capacity. Washington wants them stopped. US officials reportedly tied intelligence sharing to a halt in refinery strikes, and US President Donald Trump called their resumption “a disgrace.”
Hours of attack before dawn
Russia’s regional alert system declared a drone threat at 03:38, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported. By 06:25, Exilenova+ said the Nikolskoye station was under attack, after Michurinsk had been under attack for several hours.
Pervyshov said four Ukrainian drones were shot down over the region and no one was hurt. He did not name the site.
Ukraine has not commented. The General Staff’s 20 October list of overnight strikes does not mention Tambov Oblast.
A Druzhba fuel hub hit before
The Nikolskoye station belongs to Transneft, Russia’s state pipeline operator. It stores and pumps crude oil and refined fuels, including diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel. The complex has three tank farms and two pumping stations, and it can move up to 300,000 tonnes a day, according to Current Time.
Ukrainian drones hit a station of the same hub in August 2025, and Ukraine’s General Staff said then that pumping on the pipeline had stopped completely.
Strikes resume despite US pressure
Ukraine paused refinery strikes for three days after Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October, while Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid. Since Kyiv resumed the strikes, drones have also hit an oil terminal and a fuel depot in St. Petersburg.
Kyiv reads other US moves as pressure too, from missed warnings of Russian ballistic launches to a Starlink cap that slows Ukrainian drones. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy told US senators he had offered a 30-day halt on refinery strikes in exchange for Patriot interceptors, but Trump’s envoys showed no openness.

articles.title: South Korea will pull staff from Kyiv over North Korean POW handover made public at the UN
articles.body:
South Korea will withdraw more staff from its embassy in Kyiv, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon said on 20 October. Seoul says Kyiv broke an understanding to keep the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war confidential, which was meant to protect the soldiers and their families in the North. Seoul had conveyed its position through several channels but received no sufficient response from Kyiv, Park added.
The Korea Herald noted, the move comes amid a dispute with the host government itself. That matters beyond the two countries. Good ties with Kyiv serve South Korea’s interests, AP reported earlier this month, citing experts, because Ukraine could share intelligence on North Korea’s expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experience.
Seoul shrinks its Kyiv mission
Officials put the planned withdrawal at about half the embassy’s staff. The Korea Herald added that the timing has yet to be set. A chargé d’affaires and all consular staff will stay in Kyiv to keep diplomatic contacts and protect South Korean citizens.
Zelenskyy told the UN General Assembly in September that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea. Ukrainian forces had captured both men in Russia’s Kursk Oblast in January 2025, where Pyongyang had sent troops to fight for Moscow.
Ukraine’s disclosure of secret North Korean POW transfer sparks South Korea’s demand for an apology
On 6 October, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Sybiha’s messages included words of apology but fell short of what Seoul expected. Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi replied that Sybiha had written he regretted the situation reaching an exchange of critical comments.
In an interview published on 12 October, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told the dispute stemmed from differing readings of confidentiality at various stages of the transfer. He considers the matter closed. “Ukraine fulfilled all its obligations.”

articles.title: Without US intelligence, Ukraine cannot counter ballistic missiles — lawmaker
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. Without US intelligence, Ukraine is unable to counter ballistic missiles, and Kiev’s European allies will not be able to make up for American aid, member of Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada (parliament) Alexey Goncharenko (listed in Russia as extremist and terrorist) said.
"Last night I heard ballistic missiles coming in <...> all night long. And we heard that there were only incoming missiles, but no outgoing ones (referring to the operation of Ukrainian air defense systems). We have nothing to shoot down ballistic missiles with without the Americans. What’s more, as it turns out, without the Americans, we don’t even know when they take off or where they’re headed. All the talk about our own intelligence - and that the Europeans will cover for American intelligence for us - turned out to be false. No one can replace American intelligence," he said in an interview with RBC-Ukraine.
The lawmaker criticized Ukrainian politicians, including Vladimir Zelensky, for making accusations in the media against US President Donald Trump. "Under such circumstances, a responsible politician has no right to attack the American president," he added.
Previously, Ukrainian military officials and politicians had repeatedly said that the United States was not fully providing data on ballistic missile launches, preventing Ukrainian air defense systems from effectively intercepting them.

articles.title: South Korea pulls diplomats from Ukraine
articles.body:
South Korea pulls diplomats from Ukraine
South Korea is withdrawing more diplomatic staff from Ukraine over Kiev’s failure to resolve a dispute sparked by Vladimir Zelensky’s disclosure of a secret North Korean prisoner transfer, the Foreign Ministry in Seoul has announced.
The dispute erupted after Zelensky publicly announced the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul during his address to the UN General Assembly in September. South Korea insists that the operation was supposed to remain confidential, while Ukrainian authorities deny that any such agreement existed.
The servicemen were reportedly captured in January 2025 in Russia’s Kursk Region, where North Korean troops helped Russian forces repel a Ukrainian incursion.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Park Doo-soon announced the withdrawal at a press briefing on Tuesday, saying that Kiev had failed to take “positive steps” to settle the dispute despite repeated diplomatic protests.
“This measure was taken because we judged it necessary to facilitate an amicable resolution of the issue and restore trust between the two countries,” Park told reporters.
He also cited persistent threats of airstrikes across Ukraine, saying they had made it difficult to guarantee the safety of diplomatic personnel.
Seoul did not disclose how many staff would be withdrawn. A chargé d’affaires will remain in Kiev to maintain diplomatic contacts, while consular personnel will continue assisting South Korean nationals.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung accused Kiev of violating a confidentiality agreement intended to protect the prisoners and their families in North Korea. He warned that exposing the transfer could endanger their relatives and undermine stability on the Korean Peninsula, insisting that Ukraine itself had originally demanded secrecy.
Earlier this month, Lee warned that “if the Ukrainian government continues to refuse acknowledging the facts and issuing a public apology, we will take additional measures.”
The row deepened after Zelensky’s adviser Dmitry Litvin denied that any confidentiality agreement existed. Seoul summoned Ukraine’s acting ambassador to lodge a formal protest and demanded that Kiev acknowledge the arrangement and issue a public apology.
South Korea recalled its ambassador from Kiev on October 8 after its demands went unanswered. The move marked the first time in 18 years that Seoul had withdrawn an ambassador in a diplomatic protest. The latest decision further escalates the standoff, with South Korean media reporting that roughly half of the embassy staff are now expected to leave Kiev.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga previously sought to downplay the row with Seoul, describing it as a “diplomatic misunderstanding” and saying that he was working to resolve it. He denied that Kiev had breached its commitments, attributing the dispute to differing interpretations of confidentiality arrangements.
Last week, Sibiga declared the matter closed, insisting Ukraine had fulfilled all its obligations. Seoul, however, said a message from Kiev containing words of apology fell short of what it expected.
South Korea has become a major arms exporter since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, securing multibillion-dollar weapons deals with Poland. However, Seoul has refused to supply lethal weapons directly to Kiev, citing its longstanding policy against arming countries at war.
It has instead provided non-lethal military equipment, including helmets, bulletproof vests, and mine detectors, alongside humanitarian and financial aid.

articles.title: Rubio outraged by claims US no longer warns Ukraine of ballistic threats
articles.body:
Rubio outraged by claims US no longer warns Ukraine of ballistic threats
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed reports that the United States has stopped transmitting data on ballistic threats to Ukraine as false.
Source: European Pravda, citing Rubio speaking to journalists in India
Details: Rubio insists that the lack of warning about the launch of Russian ballistic missiles against Ukraine was an "internal issue" rather than a deliberate move by the US administration.
Quote: "I saw somebody associated with the Ukrainian government say that people in Ukraine are dying because the US is denying them information. That's scandalous. That's outrageous. That's just simply not true. That's not accurate."
Details: Rubio noted that he was referring to the Russian attacks on 13 and 18 October. The US is currently investigating the nature of the problem with the warnings.
Quote: "Now, that there was a problem identifying that, perhaps there was an internal issue in terms of them being able to take the information that was being provided and systematise it and react to it. That's possible. We're looking at it. Our understanding is that to the extent that happened on the 13th and on the 18th, it was a technical matter.
It was not the result of any sort of US directive not to provide advance warning of a strike. And we are providing the same warnings to them now that we always have."
Background:
- On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke with Rubio to discuss the situation regarding Starlink, warnings about ballistic attacks, and air defence assistance.
- On 18 October, Zelenskyy said the US had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine to defend against Russian missile strikes.
- Meanwhile, Rubio insisted that there had previously been "software problems" on the Ukrainian side, which caused delays in notifications regarding ballistic threats.

articles.title: Vance refuses to call Ukraine an ally
articles.body:
Vance refuses to call Ukraine an ally
Vice President J.D. Vance refused to call Ukraine a US ally, noting that the two countries are at odds on a number of issues.
Asked by journalist Mark Halperin in an interview released on Monday whether Ukraine is a US ally, Vance suggested that Kiev is “certainly a partner” but noted that the countries “have some divergent interests from time to time.” 
“Do I think they should be bombing Russian diesel facilities that raise the cost of energy for Americans? No… I think they should stop bombing Russian energy.”
Pressed on the distinction between partner and ally, Vance said the US has no formal alliance with Ukraine. “They’re not in NATO. I don’t think that they should be in NATO,” he said. He added that the two countries will continue to work on some issues despite their differences.
The remarks come amid a rift between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, which escalated after Trump announced a surprise deal to bring Russian diesel to the US and global markets following talks with President Vladimir Putin in early October.
Zelensky called the deal a “weak decision,” which came after Kiev ignored a number of US requests to stop attacking Russian refineries.
Zelensky refused to comply with Trump’s demand to end the strikes. The US president accused him of driving up fuel prices for Americans and said: “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Zelensky’s presidential term expired in May 2024, but he refused to hold a new election, citing martial law. Russia has since declared Zelensky illegitimate, saying his status is an obstacle to signing a binding peace deal.
On Sunday, Trump accused Zelensky of not wanting the conflict with Russia to end, saying he “probably never did,” adding that Ukraine should “get somebody else to negotiate.”
Ukrainian officials also reported that they missed advance US warnings of Russian missile strikes and claimed there are new restrictions on the Starshield satellite service developed by SpaceX and used by Ukrainian drones. Media reports also suggested that the US threatened to stop intelligence sharing with Kiev, which US officials have denied.

articles.title: Elon Musk ordered the Starlink restrictions that disabled Ukrainian drones, defenses - report
articles.body:
Elon Musk was behind the speed restrictions placed on the military-grade version of Starlink used by Ukrainian forces, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday night, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.
SpaceX first placed a limit on some services in Ukraine on October 13 without warning. Ukrainian officials at the time feared the move by Musk's company may have been made at the request of US President Donald Trump.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Ukraine was unable to use its interceptors against Russian drone attacks as a result of the restrictions on Saturday, saying that Ukraine had been told that they had been caused by technical issues.
Musk claims POTUS behind any decisions on speed limits as Trump denies responsibility
Trump said on Friday that he did not think he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access in a way that affected its military operations against Russia and told reporters on Monday that he didn't know who was responsible but "would like to find out."
Musk posted that "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," to his X/Twitter account shortly after the slowdown was publicized.
According to the WSJ report, some US officials said that Musk acted without any order from Trump. However, a person familiar with the situation told WSJ that Musk had communicated with multiple senior administration officials, including Trump himself, before imposing the new speed cap.
This comes amidst strained US-Ukrainian ties, with Trump accusing Zelensky of sabotaging peace efforts and Zelensky accusing the Trump administration of withholding intelligence, which the White House has denied.
"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told journalists on Tuesday.
Rubio added that he had had a 45-minute conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday. Zelensky said the topics included ballistic missile interceptors, early warning of Russian attacks and the situation with Starlink and Starshield satellite services.
Trump criticizes Zelensky's attack on Russian diesel
Trump has criticized Zelensky for attacking Russian diesel refineries, saying on October 10, days before the Starlink restrictions, that he told Zelensky, "You can do whatever you want to Russia, but don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem.’ And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel. He better damn well stop.”
Trump reiterated his criticism in a Truth Social post on Sunday, saying that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," calling on the Ukrainian leader to stop attacking Russian diesel facilities.
Musk has publicly agreed with Trump's criticism, responding to a video of Trump telling Zelensky to stop the attacks with "Zelensky has gone too far," on X, four days before drone operators reported losing unrestricted access to Starlink.
Ukraine is still “waiting for the official response from contacts with the Pentagon and SpaceX at the leaders' level to understand what has happened, but also to understand whether the connection has been restored or will be restored,” Ukraine's top diplomat in Washington, Denys Sienik, told the WSJ on Tuesday.
Amichai Stein and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Bangladesh’s Vital Garment Industry Struggles Amid Global Energy Crunch
articles.body:
It’s 11 a.m. at Ha-Meem Group’s Ashulia garment factory north of Dhaka and every floor is a whirlwind of feverish labor. Industrial jigsaws slice stacks of denim into precise panels, which nearby seamsters then stitch into jeans, skirts, and jackets.
Next comes washing, ironing, and affixing buttons and zips before the brand labels are attached—Gap, American Eagle, and JCPenney are major clients—and the finished garments are stacked into boxes by some of the group’s 90,000 staff, who together produce 9.3 million apparel items every month.
But suddenly the lights flicker, the workshop dims for a moment, and then full illumination returns accompanied by four cacophonic British-made diesel generators, which automatically splutter into life whenever the gas supply weakens.
“In Bangladesh, the grid electricity is bad, there are frequent interruptions,” says Tanul Chakraborty, head of power, energy and environmental sustainability for Ha-Meem Group. “After gas the most reliable energy in Bangladesh is diesel. Grid electricity is third. Almost the entire economy moves on diesel.”
It’s a startling admission given that Bangladesh’s economy is worth $510 billion, South Asia’s second-largest after India. But the nation is in the grip of a severe power crunch, as wars in Ukraine and Iran expose the fragility of its growing dependence on imported fuel. Since Russia’s invasion, industrial gas prices have risen by 150%, and diesel by about 70%. Since the Iran war began, the cost of spot liquefied natural gas (LNG) has nearly tripled.
That’s bad news for a garment industry that is the country’s largest source of formal employment, directly providing 4 million jobs and supporting countless more livelihoods, while generating $38.7 billion last year—over 80% of export earnings. (Ha Meem alone accounted for $1 billion of exports.)
But the strain extends across the Global South, where developing nations struggle with a prolonged energy crisis that disproportionately squeezes the planet’s most deprived. In the Philippines, heavy dependence on imported Gulf oil has forced emergency conservation measures, including four-day working weeks, restrictions on official travel, and flight cancellations. Diesel prices have risen 86% in Nigeria and more than 50% in Tanzania and Ethiopia, driving up the cost of farming, trucking, and electricity from generators—and, in turn, the price of staples such as rice and corn.
“The poorest people, who spend the highest share of their income on food and fuels, will be hit the hardest,” Indermit Gill, World Bank Chief Economist, warned in April.
In Dhaka, a sprawling megacity of almost 40 million that is usually defined by relentless momentum, the nights have grown eerily dark. With the national power shortfall exceeding 3,000 megawatts, the government has imposed sweeping cuts, exempting only essential services such as hospitals and pharmacies. Illuminated billboards along busy commercial corridors now dim soon after sunset, while shops close an hour early. The burden is even heavier in rural villages, where residents have recently endured blackouts lasting as long as 16 hours a day.
For ordinary citizens, daily life has become a relentless calculus: Residents are forced to rise before dawn in the hope that their stove's gas pressure might be strong enough to cook. Other quandaries include how long they can run a fan against the suffocating humidity, and how far the queues will stretch at the gas station. As businesses flounder, a secondary crisis looms: global malnutrition monitors warn that 18.1 million Bangladeshis may soon face food insecurity.
Internal missteps have only tightened external bottlenecks. The country of 175 million drastically underinvested in both transmission infrastructure and domestic gas fields, meaning today it relies on imports from the Middle East for almost half of its energy. But between July and August, imports of LNG plummeted 83% largely owing to disruption around the blockaded Strait of Hormuz as well as a blaze that temporarily disabled one of its two floating regasification terminals.
Last month, thousands of opposition supporters staged a long march to pressure Prime Minister Tarique Rahman—who only took office in February, just weeks before the Iran war broke out—to do more to tackle soaring fuel costs. “Energy is the biggest test for the new government and has become a galvanizing point for the opposition,” says Michael Kugelman, resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council.
While the global energy crisis is tied to geopolitics, Bangladesh’s woes are uniquely entwined. Rahman’s Bangladesh Nationalist Party took power following the popular ouster in 2024 of autocratic former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whom India granted sanctuary, deepening the rift between the neighbors.
Bangladesh imports roughly one-sixth of its electricity from India, which hasn’t been shy in wielding that strategic vulnerability as diplomatic leverage. Compounding the disruption, many of the key architects of national energy policy over Hasina’s 15-year reign have been placed on special duties ostensibly due to their ties to her Awami League party.
Bangladesh also finds itself hostage to shifting Great Power rivalry beyond its neighborhood. Dhaka invested $12.65 billion—chiefly via Moscow-backed loans—in its first nuclear power station in the town of Rooppur built by Russian energy giant Rosatom. The plant was supposed to begin operations in July 2024 but faced repeated delays due partly to the Ukraine war, which complicated payments to Russian banks and blocked the arrival of air and maritime cargo. After finally completing its first controlled nuclear reaction on Oct. 11, it is now expected to go into service in December, although months of staged testing will be required before it reaches a touted output of 1,200 MW.
Complicating matters, the U.S. Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act comes into force on Oct. 18, with provisions including sanctions on senior Russian officials and businesses supporting Russia’s energy sectors. This could mean Dhaka has to secure specific U.S. Treasury waivers or approved payment channels to service its plant debt and buy nuclear fuel.
Meanwhile, Washington is dangling its own alternatives. On Sept. 25, Bangladesh and the U.S. signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on strategic civil nuclear cooperation that focuses on small modular reactors. That comes on top of an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade inked in February that committed Dhaka to massive purchases of U.S. commodities, including $15 billion worth of U.S. energy products over a 15-year period.
But Bangladesh is also looking to Washington’s superpower rival. Rahman’s first overseas trip in June was to Malaysia and China. In Beijing, the two nations signed 17 agreements and other instruments to mark a “new era” of bilateral relations, with one explicitly covering renewable energy cooperation. But two of the agreements involved corporate groups subject to U.S. sanctions, and the growing ties between Dhaka and Beijing have caused consternation in Washington, State Department sources tell TIME. Bangladesh is also in advanced negotiations with a Chinese state-owned firm to build a third floating LNG terminal.
Seemingly pulled in every direction, Dhaka is desperate to instill more energy independence. The government recently launched a special incentive package for rooftop solar, slashing import duties on solar equipment from 17% to 1%, while particularly encouraging systems paired with battery storage. Bangladesh added some 200 MW of solar capacity to the national grid over the first half-year, according to government figures. However, that rate must be ramped up sixfold to have any hope of achieving ambitious five-year targets.
“We are actually looking into diversification, new areas where we can source energy from,” Shama Obaed Islam, State Minister for Foreign Affairs, told TIME as part of a panel at the 2026 Bay of Bengal Conversation last week. “We have [also] been looking into solar energy [and] making every citizen self-sufficient in energy.”
But while rooftop solar may work well for homes, it is far less useful for energy-intensive factories. Ha-Meem has 29.2 MW installed on its roofs—one of the largest private solar installations nationwide—though Chakraborty says it is only helpful for perhaps four hours per day when the sun is highest at a factory complex that operates around the clock.
Paradoxically, Ha-Meem has seen demand increase since the energy crisis. It has absorbed orders from some of the more than 400 smaller factories forced out of business in the three years till June (as well as from customers shifting production out of China to skirt Trumpian tariffs.) But with Ha-Meem’s energy bills rising from roughly $200,000 to $300,000 every day, and clients refusing to budge on prices, there is a relentless drive to boost efficiency.
In the office of Ha-Meem Senior Executive Director Brig-Gen (Ret.) Mohammad Abdul Moeen, a computer spreadsheet maps every employee against hourly targets. Workers who fall behind are counseled by managers—“maybe she had some problem with the machine,” says Moeen. “She may have just been tired”—and offered additional support and training. Those who consistently fall short are replaced by some of the dozens of applicants clutching résumés who queue up at the factory gate each morning.
“We may be facing some kind of energy crisis but that’s more reason why we cannot compromise with productivity,” says Moeen.
Moeen’s relentless focus on efficiency is easy to fathom. The garment industry is ruthlessly competitive and manufacturers fear that any rise in costs or supply disruption could see orders shift to rival Vietnam, Cambodia, or Pakistan. However, simply securing energy is not alone sufficient; with many Western brands making ambitious sustainability commitments that rely on shifting away from fossil fuels, how power is generated is also a key concern.
And if preserving Bangladesh’s dominant role in global garment production is precarious, diversifying the economy is harder still. The nation has ambitious goals of ramping up existing pharmaceutical and leather industries, and even moving into autos, medical devices, and semiconductors. But competition is tough, and few serious investors are charmed by candlelight meetings.
Last month, Bangladesh unveiled a new energy roadmap that aims to add 12,940 MW of generation capacity via new solar installations and coal-fired projects, alongside modernization of grid distribution networks and a total of 300 new exploration wells to firm up domestic gas supplies (31 have already been drilled.)
“We are satisfied with that plan,” says Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association, which represents over 2,500 garment factories. “Within three or four years, maybe there will be no more electricity crisis.”
For now, however, Bangladesh’s garment workers—and billions across the Global South—have little choice but to endure given scant signs of relief in oil markets. In recent days, Yemen’s Houthis have intensified missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, cities, and oil infrastructure, killing civilians in Riyadh, disrupting flights, and provoking Saudi-led strikes that have stoked fears of a wider regional war.
“It’s a difficult situation for the present government,” says Fazlee Shamim Ehsan, managing director of Fatullah Apparels Ltd., which produces 22,000 finished garments per day. “It would be much better if there was no war in the Middle East.”
—With reporting by Zia Chowdhury/Dhaka

articles.title: Russians try to sneak toward Zaporizhzhia through the dried-up Kakhovka Reservoir. Ukrainian intelligence captures three
articles.body:
Fighters of the Bratstvo Battalion, part of the Timur Special Unit of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR), captured three Russian servicemen and gave first aid to one of them, HUR reported on 19 October. They also found and destroyed Russian sabotage groups, HUR said, adding that counter-sabotage operations in the Zaporizhzhia direction are ongoing.
Russian forces have spent months trying to get closer to Zaporizhzhia, one of Ukraine’s largest cities. They may try to use the dried-up bed of the Kakhovka Reservoir to infiltrate north toward it as autumn fog and dense vegetation set in, the Institute for the Study of War reported on 26 September. Ukrainian troops are now clearing the area of Russian saboteurs trying to get into the rear of Ukrainian positions, according to HUR.
HUR’s video shows the fighting and the captures, with one dead Russian soldier blurred. At the end, a captured Russian says two of the three men in his group were killed by a “Baba Yaga,” the nickname Russian troops use for Ukraine’s heavy bomber drones.
HUR described what the Russian groups are trying to do:
“Using small sabotage groups, the enemy is attempting to penetrate deep into the rear positions of Ukraine’s Defense Forces, build up forces to destabilize the situation, disrupt logistics, and neutralize Ukrainian defenders’ combat crews.”
Russia seeks to bring the front closer to Zaporizhzhia
Russia’s objective in the Zaporizhzhia direction is to advance within artillery range of the city, hold forward positions, and protect its rear from Ukrainian strikes, the Institute for the Study of War noted.
In January, Russian forces were trying to capture Stepnohirsk and advance along the shore of the former Kakhovka Reservoir toward Zaporizhzhia. Taking the settlement would let Russian troops place long-range artillery or fiber-optic drones there to strike the city’s outskirts, Southern Defense Forces spokesperson Vladyslav Voloshyn told Ukrinform on 14 January.
Russia drained the Kakhovka Reservoir. Now it hides in the dry bed to creep toward Zaporizhzhia
On 22 September, Anastasiia Shevchenko, spokesperson for the Southern Forces Group, said there were no signs of preparations for a direct offensive on Zaporizhzhia and that Russian forces lacked the troops and means to advance directly toward the city.
Dense vegetation and limited visibility: combat on the reservoir bed
The Kakhovka Reservoir was a vast artificial body of water on the Dnipro River in southern Ukraine that supplied water to millions of people, as well as to agriculture and industry. On 6 June 2023, Russian forces blew up the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant, the Southern Operational Command reported.
After the dam was destroyed, the bed of the former reservoir quickly became overgrown with willows, poplars, and shrubs, creating a new battlefield. Ukrainian troops have fought there before.
In November 2025, fighters from the same Bratstvo unit carried out a reconnaissance and sabotage operation 7 kilometers from the shoreline of the former reservoir, HUR said. They found and eliminated Russian troops, then raised the Ukrainian flag over the islands there and took control of the area.
In April, the Bratstvo unit’s chief of staff, who goes by the call sign “Dyviziia,” described the conditions on an earlier raid across the reservoir bed:
“You’re just constantly moving through these thickets, with no way to figure out which direction to go. You can literally see everything just two meters ahead of you.”

articles.title: Slovenian Company Unveils Anti-Drone System Based on War-Proven Turret in Ukraine
articles.body:
The Ljubljana-based company Valhalla Turrets, which specializes in remote-controlled weapon stations (RCWS), announced the Skythunder counter-unmanned aircraft systems (C-UAS) system on X on Friday.
The Skythunder is based on the MANGART 25 turret, whose first prototypes were sent to Ukraine for direct field testing. It was provided as part of the Wolf 25 AD C-UAS system manufactured in partnership with the Slovak defense company DefTech to meet a Ukrainian C-UAS requirement in early 2025.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The system replaces the Oerlikon KBA 25mm automatic cannon in the Wolf 25 AD with the three-barrel GDLS 20mm M197 Gatling gun – the main armament normally mounted on the AH-1Z Viper attack helicopter.
The M197 weighs about 60 kilograms (132 pounds), fires up to 1,500 rounds per minute, and has a maximum effective range of about 2,000 meters (2,200 yards).
The gun is paired with a 70mm (2.75-inch) laser-guided rocket launcher that provides longer-range precision strike capabilities than the Gatling gun. This could be the Arnold Defense LAND-LGR4 “Fletcher” system that is fitted to other Valhalla Turrets weapons. This could extend the effective range out to 5-7 kilometers (3-4.4 miles).

The image released on X shows the system mounted directly on an Oshkosh 6x6, 5-ton FMTV M1140 chassis – the same platform used by the M142 HIMARS multi-barreled rocket system.
The incorporation of these critical US-sourced components has led commentators to suggest that Skythunder was intended to compete for the Pentagon’s “Low, Slow, Small Unmanned Aircraft Integrated Defeat System (LIDS),” the first $729 million contract of which US arms maker RTX Raytheon recently won.
Russian Drone Strike Near Kyiv-Odesa Highway Kills 3
According to the Valhalla Turrets announcement, Skythunder features integrated 360-degree radar coverage, which allows it to autonomously sense, track, and engage large swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) as part of an integrated air defense network.
Other Valhalla Turrets-based systems
In October 2025, Croatian arms maker DOK-ING and Valhalla Turrets produced the KOMODO-MANGART 25 unmanned C-UAS system. The fully robotic platform is designed for urban operations, infrastructure protection and high-risk operations, according to a DOK-ING press release covered by Ukrainian tech outlet dev.ua.
In the same month, Valhalla Turrets and Azerbaijani defense firm Zireh unveiled the HMS30 mobile C-UAS system at the ADEX 2026 defense exhibition in Baku, Azerbaijan.
The HMS30 is mounted on a KamAZ-43114 military truck chassis and fields twin Russian-designed 30mm 2A42 automatic cannons. It uses an advanced electro-optical sighting system and has a range of 1.5 to 2 kilometers (0.9 to 1.2 miles).
In June, the company presented the Skythunder 300 at the Eurosatory 2026 exhibition. The Skythunder 300 is based on the MANGART 30 remote weapon control system (RWCS) and was mounted on a Daimler 4x4 armored truck.
It included a Northrop Grumman MK44S Bushmaster 30mm automatic cannon, a separate turret mounting a Dillon Aero M134D 7.62mm six-barrel machine gun, and Arnold Defense LAND-LGR4 70mm guided rockets.
In August, General Dynamics European Land Systems integrated a Valhalla MANGART 30 turret into its ASCOD tracked combat vehicle.
Austrian Spanish Cooperation Development (ASCOD) is a family of modular, tracked armored fighting vehicles developed jointly by Austrian Steyr-Daimler-Puch AG and Spanish General Dynamics Santa Bárbara Sistemas (part of General Dynamics European Land Systems).
According to the Israeli Defense news site, gun-based air defense systems will be an essential component of the West’s C-UAS capabilities. It says the war in Ukraine has demonstrated an urgent operational need for a more cost-effective way of intercepting large numbers of low-cost drones, rather than current, expensive interceptor missiles that cost significantly more than the targets they face.

articles.title: US Restores Intelligence to Ukraine as Witkoff Carries Peace Proposals to Putin
articles.body:
US intelligence sharing with Ukraine for early warnings of Russian attack is working again, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday, Oct. 20, following talks in Oslo, Norway. Kyiv had spent a week already without US intelligence ahead of the meeting.
“We are thankful that intelligence works now,” Zelensky said. “I think we will have good results.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Following talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Zelensky said Ukraine could see results within the next 48 hours on Patriot interceptors, intelligence sharing and Starlink restrictions.
He described the conversation as substantive and positive, with both sides agreeing on the next steps.
Witkoff to visit Moscow with fresh proposals
Senior US envoy Steve Witkoff is set to travel to St. Petersburg to present Russia’s leadership with proposals drawn up during talks with Ukrainian and European leaders in Oslo on Tuesday, Oct. 20, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
Støre spoke during a joint news conference with Zelensky and Finnish President Alexander Stubb following a meeting with Witkoff. Ukraine’s security, its postwar prosperity, territorial questions and sanctions were covered during the discussion.
Zelensky said the sides discussed several types of security guarantees set out in a draft document. The proposals would be passed to the Russian side and Kyiv would then wait for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s response.
Witkoff attended in person, while his negotiating partner Jared Kushner joined by video after falling ill with the flu, Norwegian newspaper VG reported.
Japan Lifts 5-Year Restrictions on Ukrainian Poultry, Egg Imports
“All of us want peace, and we will see what will be tomorrow,” Zelensky said.
Moscow signals openness to US proposals – rules out concessions
The Kremlin, for its part, signaled openness to US proposals, but strictly ruled out concessions of territory.
“We’ll see what they propose,” Russia’s Foreign Miniser Sergey Lavrov said, according to Russian state-owned media TASS.
“If they propose something that benefits us economically and financially then why not? But it should not involve any political concessions on our part,” he continued.
Moscow has long demanded that Ukraine withdraw from the parts of Donetsk region it still controls and cede the entire territory, give up its bid to join NATO and accept limits on the size of its armed forces.
Kyiv, however, has repeatedly rejected having to give up its territorial sovereignty as part of any possible peace settlement.
Zelensky points to Russian support for Iran
Asked about US President Donald Trump’s reluctance to put too much pressure on Putin due to fears that Moscow could increase its backing for Iran, Zelensky said he could not say whether Putin was using Iran as leverage.
He did say that Ukraine had seen evidence of Russian drone components delivered to Iran and said Russian satellite intelligence was being shared with Tehran.
“I know that Russia stays on the side of Iranians,” Zelensky said.
Leaders urge focus on the future
Zelensky, Stubb and Støre stressed that no decisions about Ukraine’s future should be made without Kyiv at the table. Støre urged participants to set aside the heated rhetoric of recent days and focus on the path ahead, and Stubb agreed.
Zelensky thanked Norway for hosting the talks, calling it one of the countries doing the most to help Ukraine protect lives.
“Ukraine wants peace more than anyone. It was Russia that started this war,” Zelensky said.
Peace push resumes after a week of diplomatic tensions
After more than a week of tensions between Kyiv and Washington, diplomacy appears to be gaining momentum again.
The latest round of shuttle diplomacy began on the weekend of Sept. 5–6. Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow and then traveled to Kyiv the next day, in what marked their first visit to Ukraine despite repeated trips to Russia.
Although all three sides – the US, Russia and Ukraine – described the meetings as positive and substantive, no breakthrough was reached in ending Russia’s aggression.
Relations deteriorated after Trump struck an abrupt diesel deal with Putin on Oct. 9, on the same day that Ukrainian delegation was in Miami hoping to negotiate an end to the war with Trump’s administration.
Ukraine then faced restrictions on Starlink terminals without prior warning and a week-long pause in US intelligence sharing, although US officials denied responsibility in either of those.

articles.body:
