Russia May Be Preparing Nuclear Weapons to Destroy Western Satellites, RUSI Warns
Russia could pursue space-based nuclear weapons capable of targeting Western military satellites, as its existing anti-satellite missile arsenal may be insufficient to disable large numbers of spacecraft during a potential war with NATO.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 20, citing a report by the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), Russia reportedly retains Soviet-era 79M6 Kontakt anti-satellite missiles designed for the specialized MiG-31D aircraft and may have the industrial capacity to produce significant numbers of A-235 Nudol interceptors.
The report suggests that Russia’s production capacity for Nudol missiles could exceed the 55 SM-3 interceptors the United States plans to manufacture by 2031.
However, even such an arsenal might not be enough to destroy large numbers of Western reconnaissance and communications satellites in the event of a large-scale war against the West, according to Defense Express, citing RUSI.
RUSI’s assessment suggests that this limitation could push Moscow toward developing specialized satellites capable of carrying nuclear weapons into space, potentially allowing Russia to threaten multiple spacecraft rather than relying exclusively on conventional missile interceptors.
The A-235 Nudol system was originally developed for Moscow’s missile defense network, but its anti-satellite capabilities were demonstrated in 2021, when Russia destroyed one of its own satellites during a weapons test.
Meanwhile, the operational status of the Soviet-era Kontakt system remains uncertain. Although Russia announced plans to revive the program and photographs of a MiG-31 carrying a suspected anti-satellite missile emerged in 2018, there is no publicly confirmed evidence that the system entered active service.
In April 2026, US Space Force Commander General Steven Whiting warned that Russia could deploy nuclear anti-satellite weapons in low Earth orbit, potentially triggering what he described as a “space Pearl Harbor.” Such an attack could disable thousands of satellites, disrupting GPS, communications, and military reconnaissance systems.

articles.title: US AI centers will be targeted in next war: MP
articles.body:
Alaeddin Boroujerdi, a member of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, said one of the key areas of US interests in the region is investment in new technologies and artificial intelligence, and that these centers will definitely be targeted in any possible next war.

He said membership means Iran is committed not to build a nuclear bomb.
He said withdrawal from the NPT would mean "no commitment not to build a nuclear bomb," and that any country choosing to leave the treaty would face broad political consequences. He said removing the commitment not to build an atomic bomb means entering a phase of nuclear weapons development, and that NPT withdrawal is a lever Iran must use in its discourse.
He said the consequences are significant, but if such a decision is ever made, it must be made with its requirements, and the Supreme National Security Council is the body that naturally determines such matters.
On the details of the US response to Iran's seven conditions, Boroujerdi said that as far as he knows, the conditions have been accepted but the US has added its own conditions. He said he does not have exact information but believes the US conditions certainly concern the nuclear issue and the delivery or dilution of 60%-enriched nuclear material.
Boroujerdi said the Americans have no choice but to accept Iran's conditions, because they have defined interests in the Arab countries on the shores of the Persian Gulf, and Iran will certainly not allow the US to have its former presence in the region.
Referring to recent threats by Trump to launch a military attack on Iran, Boroujerdi said one of the key areas of US interests in the region is investment in new technologies and artificial intelligence, and that all these interests and centers are under Iran's surveillance and will definitely be targeted in any possible next war. He said the Americans would then understand who is the loser and who is the winner.
Asked whether placing Iran under the nuclear umbrella of countries such as China and Russia is on the agenda, Boroujerdi said that given the Islamic Republic's current standing and its national and Islamic dignity, as a country that, he does not think the system's policy is to place itself under the security umbrella of even its friends.

articles.title: Chemical brother: Russia’s production of explosives and ammunition is heavily dependent on Chinese chemicals
articles.body:
Russia’s explosives production relies heavily on imported chemicals from China. The Insider identified the key reagents used by Russia’s defense industry, the foreign companies supplying them, and the chemicals most critical to explosives production — including plasticizers, binders, acids, and stabilizers.
The Insider has previously reported that Russia’s chemical industry remains heavily dependent on foreign equipment, technology, and catalysts. That reliance is especially pronounced in the defense sector, where ammunition production depends on imported auxiliary components.
According to the available data, Russia imported more than $1 billion worth of chemical products in the first quarter of 2025, totaling 347,000 metric tons. China accounted for 87% of those imports, followed by Indonesia and India. The statistic accounts for imported chemicals but does not make a distinction between shipments that were intended for civilian or military use; however, many of the chemicals imported have clear military uses.
Components for explosives
Plasticizer
Explosives are central to modern warfare, and producing plastic explosives from RDX or HMX requires a binder, or plasticizer. One such plasticizer is dioctyl sebacate, which Russian manufacturers produce using imported sebacic acid.
In 2025, the Roshal Plasticizer Plant bought sebacic acid from Chinese supplier Farmasino Co., Ltd. As customs records show, the plant specified that the chemical was intended for production of dioctyl sebacate rather than for pharmaceutical use.
Binders
One binder used in explosives and imported by Russia is polyisobutylene. It is brought into the country in a form that is ready for use in explosives production.
In 2025, the Azot-Vzryv group purchased polyisobutylene in China from Nanjing E-Strong Technical Co., Ltd., through a Kazakh intermediary, Nartas LLP of Almaty. Azot-Vzryv has long supplied the Sverdlov Plant, a major Russian defense chemical enterprise in Dzerzhinsk, Nizhny Novgorod region. As far as is known, the plant is virtually the only Russian producer of military high explosives based on RDX.
Additionally, a polymer made from butadiene and acrylonitrile is used as a binder in solid rocket propellant. The Perm Gunpowder Plant consumes about 1,600 metric tons of acrylonitrile every six months. Of that amount, 600 tons reach Russia from Belarus, from a plant in Novopolotsk.
Acetic acid
Acetic acid is also needed to synthesize RDX. In Russia, it is produced in Nevinnomyssk. Since Nevinnomyssky Azot is the only Russian producer of high-purity synthetic acetic acid, it is regularly targeted by Ukrainian drones. Chinese supplies help fill the gap, accounting for about 20% of deliveries.
Dozens of tons of nonfood-grade acetic acid were ordered by the Altai Region’s Pioneer Trade LLC (which has taken part in tenders to supply the Perm Gunpowder Plant) and by Bina Group LLC (a regular supplier to the Perm Gunpowder Plant and NMZ Iskra, which manufactures fuzes). The acid was supplied by Chinese companies Eli-X (Qingdao) Chem Co. and Taizhou Ruibai Chemical Co.
Stabilizers
Diphenylamine is needed to prevent nitrocellulose propellant from degrading. It is used as a stabilizer and is produced from aniline. China supplies a significant share of Russia’s needs for the substance.
As The Insider reported last year, Chinese chemical producer Jiangsu Feiya Chemical Industry was among the companies supplying diphenylamine to Russia, with buyers including firms in St. Petersburg and Bashkortostan.
Fibers and composites
Composite materials are widely used in modern weapons. Their production requires aniline, which is then used to make aramid fibers.
One major Russian recipient of aniline is SPG-Kompozit. The company makes composite shelters for radar and navigation systems, polymer ammunition containers, and modular military structures.
Aramid fibers are also needed for missile bodies. For environmental and economic reasons, aniline production in Russia virtually ceased after 2016, but the authorities are trying to restart it. For example, Alfa-Bank has allocated 11.9 billion rubles ($143.8 million) to launch an innovative aniline plant based at Chapaevsk Aniline Plant JSC.
For now, however, Russia continues to import aniline and aniline derivatives from China. The main suppliers are Jilin Kangxin Chemical Industry Trade, Shandong S-Sailing Chemical, and Shandong Near Chemical. Buyers include SPG-Kompozit LLC, SZ HK AK Bars-Development LLC, and Albatros LLC.
Other chemicals important to the military industry
Among the main imported reagents used in Russia’s chemical and related industries (including both civilian and military production) are raw materials and additives for polymers, synthetic fibers, plastics, and rubber.
Antioxidants and flame retardants are particularly important in this sector because they are generally among the most difficult products to manufacture domestically.
Russia also imports large quantities of alcohols, including propyl alcohol and methallyl alcohol, as well as other substances such as butyl glycol, methyl ethyl ketone, perchloroethylene, and dimethyl sulfoxide. They are generally used without chemical modification — either in pure form or as ingredients in more complex products.
Surfactants and flotation agents used in mining and oil production are also important for export-oriented industries.
Who supplies the chemicals
Chinese companies supply virtually all of these chemicals to Russia. In most cases, they also manufacture the products themselves.
Despite repeated calls for developing domestic production capabilities, Russia’s chemical industry remains heavily dependent on foreign suppliers, particularly for medium- and small-volume specialty chemicals. As a result, the more effectively Ukrainian drones are able to strike chemical production facilities inside Russia, the greater the dependence on imports becomes.
China’s role is critical, particularly when it comes to Russia’s access to plasticizers, antioxidants, flame retardants, and other polymer additives.

articles.title: Nato increases Black Sea deployment amid escalating deadly Russian attacks
articles.body:
Nato is deploying additional military assets to the Black Sea amid the recent deadly escalation of Russian attacks on merchant shipping, as five more vessels were attacked on Tuesday.
Russia’s military said it struck three cargo vessels in Ukraine’s port of Reni and two other cargo vessels en route to Odesa.
Russia’s targeting of vessels taking grain and other agricultural cargoes from Ukraine’s ports – central to the country’s economy – have brought the conflict to Nato’s borders, with a new high-risk designation used by the London shipping insurance market now covering all of the Black Sea save for the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey.
With a sharply rising death toll among civilian seafarers that has made Black Sea routes the world’s most dangerous, Nato announced the defensive military alliance would add more surveillance assets in the region.
Nato’s spokesperson, Allison Hart, said: “Today, Nato ambassadors met in the North Atlantic Council to discuss security in the Black Sea. Nato has already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone capabilities. Nato will be sending additional assets to the region, including support for surveillance, reconnaissance, and forensics.”
The deployment will include maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, drones and intelligence personnel. There is mounting anxiety about the increasing overspill from Russia’s war on Ukraine and the potential for further friction with Nato.
Concern has been growing after alleged Russian attacks that have increasingly edged into the territorial waters and exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria and Romania. Romania deployed jets over the weekend to shoot down two suspected Russian drones over its territory.
Romania’s defence minister, Radu Miruță, said the drones were probably latest generation Russian drones, flying at speeds similar to fighter jets.
“The ones from last night were flying at 450 km/h, which leads us to think they were Russian-made Geran-4 drones with a turboprop engine,” Miruță said. “This is the first time we’ve shot down drones like these.”
Romania has recorded 35 unauthorised drone incursions so far this year, compared with nine in 2025. Romanian forces have downed six drones this year, compared with zero last year.
Last week, two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania’s Black Sea coast, the latest in a series of attacks that have highlighted the risks to commercial shipping on Nato’s eastern flank. Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine.
At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents occurred outside Nato territorial waters.
Amid mounting concern, Bulgaria has asked Nato for the deployment of combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to its territory. On 18 October, France sent a maritime reconnaissance aircraft to Romania.
The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has said there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.
Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey, said last week his company had noted a sharp increase in the tempo of attacks beginning in July. Russian forces are estimated to be responsible for 80% of them.
The recent loss of life, he suggested, had been exacerbated by “double tap” attacks involving aerial and surface drones, the latter often carrying up to half a tonne of explosive payloads. Smaller vessels that primarily use the Danube canal system have sunk rapidly.
“While attacks against merchant vessels in the Black Sea are not new, we are seeing an escalation both in terms of the number of attacks and in the geographical scope,” Alexa said.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio urged businesses to view the India-US relationship as a strategic partnership spanning technology, trade and security, saying the two countries were “perfectly aligned” on issues that would shape the 21st century, even as he acknowledged that disagreements between them would persist.Addressing a gathering of India Inc’s leading business figures at a Freedom 250 event at BKC, Rubio said the relationship between the two countries could help shape the future of the global economy, particularly as advances in artificial intelligence and quantum computing transform industries and societies.“I truly believe the relationship between US and India is defining, in many ways, in a positive way, what the 21st century can look like,” he said.The gathering included Noel Tata (Tata Trusts), Anand Mahindra (Mahindra Group), Kiran MazumdarShaw (Biocon), Ashok P Hinduja (Hinduja Group), Amit Dixit (Blackstone), Hitendra Dave (HSBC India), K Balasubramanian (Citi India) and Rahul Badhwar (JPMorgan Chase).Rubio identified emerging technologies and secure trade routes as two areas in which the countries’ interests converge. “US and India are perfectly aligned,” he said, referring to the challenge of harnessing new technologies for public benefit.
“We have the same expertise. We have the same talented people working on it, from engineers to creative thinkers and innovators.”He linked economic growth to the security of international shipping routes, arguing that businesses needed the freedom to move goods across borders and reach markets.For India and US, he said, this required “a free and secure Indo-Pacific” in which “no nation can claim dominance or ownership of international shipping lanes”.“No two nations on earth will ever be perfectly aligned on every issue,” he said. “But on the core issues that matter..., alignment between our countries is extraordinary.”The speech did not signal any immediate change in tariffs or market access.

articles.title: Iran prolongs talks in stalemate to influence US midterms, say officials
articles.body:
Iran prolongs talks in stalemate to influence US midterms, say officials
- Iran is delaying talks with the US to avoid giving Donald Trump a political win before the November midterm elections, officials say.
- Tehran fears more US and Israeli attacks and does not trust Washington, so it wants its conditions met first, including relief from the naval blockade and oil limits.
- The stalemate is hurting Iran's economy, with inflation at 73.6%, the rial down nearly 35%, and crude exports falling to zero, while analysts say the prewar status quo will not return.
AI generated
DUBAI – Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken President Donald Trump politically ahead of November’s US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran’s reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war.
Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced that the US leader was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war.
“Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war,” one of the officials said. “The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory.”
Tehran analyst Saeed Leylaz said that, by prolonging the talks, “Iran is influencing the US election without taking any unlawful action”.
The war, which began in February when the US and its ally Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump’s approval rating to a record low, as polls suggest that Americans worried about high petrol prices will punish his Republican Party in the Nov 3 congressional elections.
Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but has not offered a detailed plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route effectively closed by Iran since the war began.
Iranian attacks, both threatened and real, have kept ship traffic through the strait to a trickle, while a US maritime blockade and trade sanctions have cut off Iran’s oil export revenues and exacerbated growing domestic economic woes.
With Tehran refusing to make concessions it believes could benefit Trump politically, there is little chance of a breakthrough before the elections, the officials said.
Under pressure from Israel, Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme – which Iran says is purely peaceful but Western powers allege has military dimensions – on the table from the outset.
For its part, Tehran insists that its conditions under a “seven-day plan” must be met before nuclear negotiations begin.
It offers no prospect of giving up the leverage over Hormuz that the conflict prompted it to seize.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry and the US White House did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.
Iran cannot trust Washington, say officials
Iran’s proposal, conveyed through Qatari mediators, offered to reopen the strait within seven days, albeit under Iranian control, provided Washington lifted its maritime blockade, eased restrictions on Iranian oil exports, released frozen assets and ended hostilities on all fronts.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Oct 18 that the offer remained on the table, with messages being exchanged through mediators.
Tehran’s view that Washington cannot be trusted to commit to diplomacy stems from the attacks on Iran that have derailed previous negotiations, one Iranian official said.
In June 2025, an Israeli attack wrecked plans for a sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks in Oman.
In February, the US and Israel launched their war just after another round of talks ended, with further technical discussions scheduled.
Maintaining a state somewhere between war and peace through the US midterms allows Iran to sustain pressure on Washington while reiterating its commitment to diplomacy.
Trump has said the US will not bomb Iran again before Nov 3.
But the officials said Tehran continued to expect that bombing would resume, sooner or later.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran programme at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said the clerical establishment clearly wanted to hurt Trump politically.
“But the fundamental issue is that Tehran believes that Trump is interested in regime change... and following Israeli Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu’s policy of seeking to bring down Iran’s ruling establishment,” he said.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Netanyahu on Oct 19, three Israeli officials said, during an unannounced visit to Israel a week before a parliamentary election in which Netanyahu’s position is at risk.
Return to pre-war status impossible for Iran, says analyst
Iran’s strategy of keeping negotiations alive without rushing towards an agreement comes at a cost.
Prolonged uncertainty is weighing on Iran’s already crippled economy and wearing down public patience.
Thousands were killed at the turn of the year when security forces crushed spiralling anti-government protests.
Annual inflation hit 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Center of Iran, and the rial currency has fallen nearly 35% against the dollar since Washington reapplied its naval blockade in July.
Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 barrels per day at the start of the month, and remained there as at Oct 5, according to energy intelligence platform Vortexa.
But the leadership’s distrust of Washington extends beyond the current conflict to existential concerns.
Iran believes the US has repeatedly broken agreements even when Tehran honoured its commitments, Leylaz said, leaving little confidence that any comprehensive deal would endure.
“Reaching a sustainable deal with the US, even after the Trump administration, is no longer possible because of the deepened distrust,” Leylaz said. “Nothing will go back to the pre-war status quo.” REUTERS

articles.title: On October 18, a Ukrainian Drone Entered Lithuanian Airspace from Polish Territory
articles.body:
On the night of October 18, a Ukrainian strike drone entered Lithuanian airspace from Polish territory; it subsequently exploded and crashed in the Pasvalys District.
Defence24 and the BNS news agency reported this, citing a statement from Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius.
According to him, radar data indicates that the drone crossed the border, was carrying explosives, and is Ukrainian.
The drone flew along the border area, but the Polish military did not detect it.
Lithuanian radars first detected the aerial target at 05:47 a.m. Kyiv time. At the time of the initial detection, the object was already over Polish territory, approximately 30–40 km from the Lithuanian border, and was moving toward Lithuania.
As Defence24 reported, citing Gedrius Premenečkas, Chief of the Defense Staff of the Lithuanian Armed Forces, the Polish military did not detect the drone on its own radars. This suggests Lithuanian surveillance systems detected the object in Polish airspace before Poland did.
At 06:02 a.m., the UAV crossed the Polish-Lithuanian border, after which local residents began calling emergency services because of its engine noise. Citizen reports led authorities to assess the object as a potential threat, as it was initially perceived as a civilian aircraft without a flight plan.
At 06:40 a.m. Kyiv time, NATO scrambled fighter jets to identify the target. The crews detected the aircraft on their onboard radars, but adverse weather conditions prevented them from establishing visual contact before the object crashed.
The drone crashed in the village of Juodžioniai in the Pasvalys District, near the border with Latvia. The explosion and falling debris damaged a civilian vehicle, but no local residents were injured.
After consulting with Lithuania, Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz instructed the military to re-examine and analyze the radar recordings from that night.
According to an explanation by Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, the air defense response algorithms did not automatically trigger a strike because the object was approaching from a friendly Schengen Zone country. Had it flown in from Belarus or Russia’s Kaliningrad region, the response would have been immediate.
On October 19, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed that the drone was Ukrainian and had deviated from its route, likely due to Russian electronic warfare systems.

articles.title: UK to deploy fighter jets to help Saudis against Houthi attacks
articles.body:
UK to deploy fighter jets to help Saudis against Houthi attacks
The Ministry of Defence announced Tuesday that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighters will be deployed to the Gulf Kingdom — but stressed they will be only used in a defensive capacity.
LONDON — U.K. fighter jets will be sent to aid Saudi Arabia in defending itself against attacks on critical energy and civilian infrastructure by the Houthis.
The Iranian-backed Islamist militia group, based in civil war-hit Yemen, has been launching ballistic missile strikes on Saudi Arabia for the past few weeks, successfully hitting three airports earlier this month.
The Ministry of Defence announced Tuesday that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighters will be deployed to the Gulf Kingdom — while stressing that they will be only used in a defensive capacity.
Advertisement
U.K. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the “continuing attacks” on the U.K.’s ally are “absolutely despicable.”
“The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” he added, referencing the attacks earlier this month that killed 14 people and injured hundreds more.
Streeting said that the fighter jets will be used to protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. The U.K. will also send an Atlas A400M aircraft, used to transport the equipment, as well as military advisers.
“This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks,” Streeting said.
The MoD argued that there is a link between the conflict in the Persian Gulf and the situation domestically in the U.K., pointing to disrupted energy supplies and a subsequent rise in the cost of living.
Since Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street in July he has offered more support to Saudi Arabia. In September, he agreed to a request for air-to-air refueling of the country’s jets.
Pressed Tuesday on whether the U.K. risked being sucked into the Saudi war with the Houthis, Burnham’s official spokesperson told reporters: “I don’t accept that characterization. Our support for Saudi Arabia is considered proportionate and focused on helping them defend themselves against relentless Houthi attacks.”
They added: “Regional instability can have a serious impact at home in the U.K. We’re clear it’s in the U.K.’s economic and security interests that the Houthis do not succeed, and our approach is about defending our people, our interests, and our allies.”

articles.title: Qatar revamped its entire defence system in six hours, intelligence chief reveals
articles.body:
At Doha’s Global Security Forum, Qatar’s head of intelligence revealed how the war with Iran forced the Gulf country to urgently redeploy its defensive assets, while the US ambassador to Turkey offered new insights into a fundamental shift in Washington's presence in the Middle East.
In a rare public appearance, Qatar’s head of the Intelligence and Security Authority Brigadier General Khalid Mohammed Al-Nuaimi revealed how Qatar took the dramatic decision to redeploy its entire defensive systems in just six hours to counter Iran's war threats.
Addressing the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday, Al-Nuaimi said the redeployment was “unprecedented and successful”, based on eight months of adapting Qatar’s forces, defence capabilities, and military doctrine, which had been built for a totally different threat landscape. 
When asked about Qatar’s response to countering drones during the war, Qatar’s head of Intelligence replied that the six-hour overhaul was based on fast-moving changes to Qatar’s defence systems, both at concept level, but also in the allocation of defence assets.
“We adapted. we redeployed and we did it within six hours,” Al-Nuaimi revealed, adding that “we were caught off guard, yet we adapted rapidly, out of sheer necessity.”
Also during the Global Security Forum, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr Majed al-Ansari said the Qatar-mediated US-Iran negotiations “are ongoing and we are seeing engagement from both parties.”
“The fact that we are not hearing about it is a good sign that we are doing our job properly,” the Qatari diplomat added amid the rising tensions and concerns that the Iran war may restart.
Washington's fundamental shift in the Middle East
In addressing those worrying concerns, US ambassador to Turkey and Special Presidential Envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack told the forum that "America wants a peace deal” which would be based on “ceasefire in the straits” as well as a focus on “easing the pain on the Iranian people”.
"Prosperity is the only answer," Barrack underlined as a way out of the current standoff, adding that "we don’t need a reboot" of the previous US-Iran peace memorandum.
He identified the obstacle to a deal as a “lack of trust.”
“What has happened from the beginning of these discussions and negotiations is a lack of trust," Barrack explained, which comes down to the fact that the "IRGC does not trust the US. And the US does not trust IRGC."
The US envoy said he did not know if the Iran war was a mistake but admitted that it had “unintended consequences” and that US President Donald Trump is a "no forever wars president."
Barrack told the forum in Qatar that the US will not leave the Middle East, even if in the region “what everybody is saying: OK, I cannot rely on America to solve all my problems,” explaining that “the bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We are not leaving.”
"America is the guarantor to the world for the last 80 years and it is no longer there," the US diplomat said, explaining that "what is happening in this administration is not an abandonment, it is a message for realignment."
The US envoy appeared to contradict one of the US administration’s declared goals in launching the Iran war, which was regime change in Tehran.
Barrack spoke broadly about how the US pursued 23 regime changes across the Middle East and concluded that "every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake."
Instead, he said, the US’ goal is to "bring everybody, put them in a tent, give them coffee, put the guns and daggers on the table, and let’s figure something else out," through “patience, presence, dialogue."
In this context, the top US diplomat also commented on the escalating tensions between Israel and Turkey, saying that "my belief is Israel is way too smart to actually pick a real fight with Turkey. I don’t think Israel wants that, I know Turkey does not want that."
'Houthis are here to stay,' former MI6 chief says
Meanwhile at the forum, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr al-Ansari also reiterated his country’s position on Yemen that alongside the other Gulf nations “Qatar is supporting our brothers in Saudi Arabia in defending their sovereignty against this attack.”
Also commenting on the Yemen war, the former head of the UK’s foreign intelligence agency MI6 Sir John Sawers told the Doha Global Security Forum that “the Houthis are here to stay.
"They are not going to be defeated, and they are going to remain in control of a large part of Yemen for the foreseeable future," Sawers said.
"The Houthis have got their own national Yemen agenda," he explained, adding that the group "exposed the limited options that Saudi Arabia has in terms of dealing with" them over the last 10 years, as their efforts "to sustain an alternative government (in Yemen) have not been successful over the last 10 years."

articles.title: Ukraine Seeks Insider Tips on Networks Supplying Western Electronics to Russia’s Weapons Factories
articles.body:

Ukraine Seeks Insider Tips on Networks Supplying Western Electronics to Russia’s Weapons Factories
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) is seeking information about networks that help Russian defense manufacturers obtain foreign-made electronics and dual-use technologies despite international sanctions.
The agency has appealed to employees of manufacturing, logistics, and trading companies, as well as individuals familiar with illicit procurement schemes, to provide information that could help identify supply chains supporting Russia’s weapons production.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR, Russian military-industrial enterprises continue to acquire Western electronic components and technologies necessary for manufacturing modern weapons, despite restrictions imposed on Moscow.
To circumvent sanctions, Russian companies reportedly rely on intermediaries, shell companies, and complex supply routes passing through third countries.
Ukrainian intelligence is particularly interested in identifying foreign suppliers of microelectronics and dual-use goods, companies acting as intermediaries, and Russian manufacturers purchasing these products for weapons production.
The agency is also seeking details about transportation routes and transit countries used to deliver restricted components to Russia.
The appeal comes amid continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities. According to HUR, more than 100 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and over 400 others, including children, injured in Russian strikes over the past week.
The attacks have affected residential buildings, passenger buses, shopping and business centers, and schools, the agency reported.
HUR said information about individual suppliers, intermediaries, or transportation routes could help identify broader procurement networks and expose companies involved in circumventing international sanctions.
The agency has encouraged individuals with relevant information to submit it confidentially through its secure Main Intelligence Bot, emphasizing that even isolated details could help trace supply chains used to obtain foreign technologies for Russian weapons manufacturing.
Ukraine’s military intelligence has also previously documented the presence of foreign-made components in Russian weapons systems, including the Kometa anti-jamming navigation modules installed in missiles, attack drones, and guided aerial bombs.
According to HUR, these modules are designed to protect onboard navigation equipment from electronic warfare interference, enabling Russian weapons to maintain navigation capabilities even in environments affected by electronic countermeasures.

articles.title: Kiev ‘in panic’ over US probe into Ukraine-Mexican drug cartel links – RT reports (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Panic over US probe into Kiev’s links to Mexican cartels – RT reports (VIDEO)
Ukrainian officials are reportedly panicking after US investigators uncovered links between Mexican drug cartels and Kiev, including paid drone training for cartel members. The probe threatens to further strain the already fragile relations between Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and US President Donald Trump.
In a statement on Tuesday, Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said American law enforcement investigating the cartels had identified at least 80 members who learned to assemble and operate combat drones while serving with Ukrainian forces.
The payment for this “education” was transferred to officials close to Zelensky using proceeds from drug sales in the US, according to the SVR report obtained by RT.
The agency also noted that Zelensky’s office is aware that the presence of trained first-person-view (FPV) drone operators among drug cartels could ultimately threaten American officers combating drug trafficking along the Mexican border and damage relations with Washington.
That, coupled with the continued supply of weapons and drones from Ukraine to other parts of the world, “has become a pattern that is quite difficult to ignore,” RT correspondent Isabella Blumberg noted.
The Washington Post similarly reported last month that Mexican cartels were hiring drone operators who had fought in Ukraine and were sending members there for training. The State Department said it was working with Kiev to prevent those skills from reaching the cartels.
Mexico’s Milenio newspaper also claimed last year that members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel had received drone and urban warfare training in Ukraine.
The alleged ties have extended beyond training, with Russian intelligence reporting in June that Ukrainian security agencies were facilitating Latin American drug trafficking into Europe while the cartels helped Kiev in recruiting fighters.
US financial support for Ukraine could ultimately backfire on Washington, with foreign funded military training potentially helping Mexican cartel members acquire skills they could later use against the US, Italian war correspondent Andrea Lucidi told RT.
“Donald Trump always spoke against the Mexican cartels and the smuggling of drugs into the US,” he said in an interview on Tuesday. “The problem is that these measures against the US, the operation of Mexican cartels, are indirectly financed by you.”
The SVR has suggested that the cartel cooperation could become another “nail in the coffin” for Zelensky’s political career. Together with corruption, continued attacks on Russian refineries, and his refusal to hold elections, it could push Washington to abandon him, the agency claimed.
The allegations come amid an increasingly bitter dispute between Zelensky and Trump over Kiev’s continued strikes on Russian refineries and stalled peace negotiations.
Trump has increasingly questioned the Ukrainian leader’s true intentions regarding the conflict, stressing that he should have settled it “a long time ago” and suggesting that he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
Trump recently went as far as stating that Ukraine should “get a new president,” and said on Monday that Kiev should get someone else to negotiate peace, arguing that Zelensky “doesn’t know what he’s talking about.”

Chinese military vessels and spy drones track Keen Sword war games off Japan
Surveillance coincides with US anti-ship missiles and Japanese long-range weapons deploying near Taiwan during exercises
Three People’s Liberation Army military aircraft – two drones and a reconnaissance plane – flew through international airspace between Japanese islands into the Pacific before heading back towards mainland China on Monday, prompting Japan to scramble fighter jets, the Joint Staff Office of Japan’s defence ministry reported the same day.
In addition, a TB-001 reconnaissance and attack drone passed between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan, flew northeast as far as waters off Amami Oshima, then turned back and passed through the Miyako Strait towards mainland China, the post said.
The aircraft movements coincided with Monday’s start of “Keen Sword”, a biennial joint military exercise between Japan and the United States running until October 29 across multiple locations in Japan. The exercise will involve about 45,000 Japanese Self-Defence Forces personnel and 12,000 US troops, making it one of the biggest drills ever conducted by the two allies.

articles.title: Witkoff could meet Putin ‘soon’ – Kremlin
articles.body:
Witkoff could meet Putin ‘soon’ – Kremlin
Moscow expects US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in the near future, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said. The American mediators held talks with Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky in the Norwegian capital of Oslo on Tuesday.
Russia highly appreciates US mediation efforts, Peskov told a news briefing on Tuesday, adding that Moscow sees every meeting between Putin and Trump’s envoys as “very important and well-timed.” He did not provide any details about the exact date or place of a potential meeting but said that the Kremlin expected Witkoff to inform Moscow about the results of Tuesday’s talks with Zelensky and his European backers.
Separately, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Tuesday that Russia was willing to discuss any economic and financial initiatives Washington could put forward, provided they were “advantageous to us.” He, however, emphasized that Moscow would not make any one-sided political concessions, warning that any deals with the US might not last beyond Trump’s term in office.
“The history of the American presidency is notable for a well-established political tradition… whereby a new president is not bound by any decisions made by their predecessor,” the minister said, adding that this approach gives the US powerful “leverage” in any talks and that Moscow is well aware that Witkoff, as well as Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, could try to “arrange something” with this in mind.
Russia should not expect “some political favor to carry us through all global affairs,” Lavrov stated. “We must rely solely on ourselves.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who hosted the meeting between Zelensky and the American negotiators, said that Witkoff would be traveling to St. Petersburg on Wednesday for a meeting with the Russian leadership.
According to Store, the list of proposals Trump’s special envoy could put forward might include a three-way summit between Trump, Putin and Zelensky. Ukrainian media also reported that other potential proposals included an energy ceasefire.
Last week, the Financial Times reported that Washington had proposed unfreezing billions of euros in Russian assets held in the EU to give impetus to Ukraine peace talks during negotiations in Miami with officials from Ukraine, France, Germany, Britain, the EU, and NATO. The idea was vehemently opposed by Kiev’s European backers, including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Russia has repeatedly identified the stance of Kiev’s European backers as one of the main obstacles to settling the conflict. The EU is still clinging to the idea of “strategically defeating Russia,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov reiterated last month.
Moscow has also rejected the idea of a temporary truce, insisting on a long-term peace deal that addresses the root causes of the conflict. With negotiations stalling and no breakthrough in sight, Ukraine has maintained its megaphone diplomacy, publicly calling for new negotiations and demanding an unconditional ceasefire.
The renewed diplomatic push follows a spat between Trump and Zelensky over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities. The American president has repeatedly demanded that Kiev stop the attacks, blaming them for surging fuel prices globally and in the US. The dispute has since widened, with Zelensky accusing Washington of withholding intelligence on Russian missile attacks and restricting Ukraine’s access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network.

articles.title: Europe Needs to Follow Zelensky’s Lead in Challenging Washington’s Appeasement
articles.body:
The latest big news is of a possible trilateral meeting between Presidents Trump, Xi, and Putin to conclude a potential Ukraine “peace” deal. Seemingly, according to a WSJ article, Putin offered Trump such a mini summit in their call on Oct. 9 - that’s the call at which a Russia-US diesel deal was thrashed out. The idea is that the three leaders meet on the sidelines of the scheduled APEC summit slated for 18-19 Nov. in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.
The Trump administration has yet to confirm whether Trump has agreed to take up Putin’s offer of a summit meeting. But the signs are ominous, as it’s on the back of a long list now of actions by Trump that smack of appeasement of Russia – from bringing Putin out of the Western freeze and inviting him to the Anchorage summit, the diesel deal as above, and this week also announcing a delay in the rollout of the Lindsay Graham sanctions bill. It also comes after the U.S. seems to have limited intelligence sharing with Ukraine that has hampered Ukraine’s defense and cost lives.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Trump has tried to explain all this away as not wanting to do anything that risked Putin pulling away from peace talks on Ukraine.
The harsh reality, though, is that Trump has now established a clear track record of pulling punches on President Putin – from his entire second term in office, and indeed before. And yet, this seems to have achieved very little, despite numerous rounds of peace talks, including those run by Messrs. Witkoff and Kushner.
CARTOON: The Ghost of True Republicanism Haunts Today’s Imposter
Remember here that Trump suggested that cutting a Ukraine peace plan would be easy, and he could get the two sides to agree within weeks of taking office for his second term, then by Easter 2025, then by year-end 2026, and here we now are close to the end of 2026, and Trump’s appeasement of Putin seems to have achieved absolutely nothing.
Worse than that, I think it has emboldened Putin to prolong the war, as he thinks that with Trump in office, the Western alliance in defense of Ukraine will inevitably collapse, offering him up the whole of Ukraine on a plate. And the latter has always been Putin’s ambition.
It gets more war, and unfortunately Ukraine has ended up paying the price in more blood and lives lost. Now Trump seems to just be repeating the prior mistakes of Schroeder, Hollande, Merkel, Macron et al.
And the latest gift to Putin is a wet dream for Putin, a great power summit, as he will see it, where Russia, China, and the US can do what great powers do – divide up the world into spheres of influence. This would be Putin’s Yalta II.
Trump is either ignorant of history or uncaring of the fate of Ukraine and Europe. For Trump, the win is just appearing on the same stage as Xi and Putin, and a place in summit history, albeit I would add ignominy, rather as was the case for Chamberlain in 1938 over Czechoslovakia.
The only problem for Trump with this Yalta 2 is that, with no Ukraine or Europe represented, I don’t see how it can deliver a meaningful peace in the war in Ukraine.
Trump might agree to Putin’s terms that Ukraine needs to deliver the rest of Donbas to Ukraine, but I cannot see Zelensky agreeing to that unless Trump is willing to offer, in exchange, cast-iron security guarantees that if Putin breaks any such agreement the US will then go to war with Russia to defend the rest of Ukraine.
Trump is never going to offer any such security assurance, and even if he did, I don’t think the Ukrainians would trust it, since they don’t trust Trump and don’t really trust such an assurance after being let down over the Budapest Memorandum in 1994.
The Ukrainians also don’t trust Putin, as they assume, quite rightly, that this war was never about Donbas, but Putin’s desires for the whole of Ukraine. So they assume that once they surrender their fortress defense in Donbas – defended valiantly over 12 years now – Putin would take them and just drive on further into Ukraine.
Politically, also, for Zelensky, surrendering Donbas, with no serious security guarantees – and likely not NATO or EU membership – would be political suicide at home. It would likely provoke a social and political revolution (remember the Orange Revolution and then Euromaidan, so Ukraine has formed here), or even a coup, destabilizing Ukraine to Russia’s advantage. And that is why Putin continues to demand something – the surrender of Donbas – which he knows that Zelensky cannot seriously agree to.
The onus will then be on Putin to secure delivery on that agreement. But there, I don’t think his military is in much of a position to then take what Trump has gifted him. If they have failed to take the Donbas in 12 years of bitter fighting, why would we assume anything different from a mere sharpie signature from Trump?
And the downside for Putin is that any constraint on Ukraine in this war will be removed. Ukraine will surely then have an interest in maximum escalation – taking the war fully to Russia and hence launching all-out deep-strike drone attacks on Russian energy infrastructure. That is hardly likely to suit Trump or Xi, as it will have severe global market impact.
Unfortunately, the outlook for Ukraine in most likely scenarios now is grim – and I would argue because Trump has mismanaged the whole Ukraine peace process. It suggests a scenario either where Putin still thinks that he can take whatever Trump offers in China and demands more, plays the long war through to the French presidential election and the assumption European support for Ukraine caves after a Le Pen win, or Ukraine is left to reject any peace deal signed by Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen but is then forced to battle on with no US support and likely strained European support.
Xi and Europe, to the rescue?
Trump and Putin likely want to exclude Europe from any such Ukraine peace talks. Xi may well too, albeit in the bigger scheme of things: does Xi want to risk signing up to a peace deal that neither Trump nor Putin can easily or quickly deliver on the ground, and that could see Ukrainian escalation to global markets, while also risking annoying European trade partners? Perhaps not.
Europe should remember here that it has agency and should impress this on both Trump and Xi. Whatever is agreed at Shenzhen, Europe has an interest in continuing to back Ukraine, given the existential threat from Russia and the US. under Trump AWOL in defending Europe; Ukraine now represents Europe’s best chance of buying time until it develops its own autonomous defense capability.
Indeed, I would have thought that Xi would not view any Trump-Putin deal over Ukraine that favorably if it opened the way then for a new special relationship between the US and Russia, a reverse Nixonian ultimately to screw over China. I would then have thought China and Europe have common interests in working together to forestall any Trump-Putin bromance consummated over Ukraine.
While playing China towards its interests over Ukraine, I think that Ukraine is such an existential interest for Europe that the latter needs to follow Zelensky in spelling out to Trump what his surrender of Ukraine to Putin would mean for the Transatlantic relationship.
They need to spell out that this would mean the end of NATO, and that Europe would be forced to fast-track efforts to develop a defense capability separate from the US. American companies would risk losing the milking-cow defense deals they have grown accustomed to.
It would also mean that Europe would not be a natural ally for the US in its ongoing hegemonic battle with China, and indeed, European defense companies would begin to compete more aggressively with their US counterparts. Net, net, this would mean a loss of US jobs and long-term damage to the US economy and ultimately its security.
Zelensky has confronted US appeasement; maybe Europe needs to do that too.

articles.title: Russia resumes diesel exports to Türkiye, Brazil, after Trump lifts sanctions on fuel supplies, boosting Moscow’s war revenue – Reuters
articles.body:
Russian diesel shipments are returning to Türkiye and Brazil after Moscow lifted its export ban and the US temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian fuel supplies, Reuters reported on 20 October, citing shipping data from Kpler and LSEG.
The resumption of exports gives Russia another source of revenue to support its war against Ukraine, allowing Moscow to profit from fuel sales despite the domestic shortages that prompted its export ban. The US sanctions relief is helping Russia restore access to international buyers while its full-scale invasion continues.
According to Reuters, at least two tankers carrying Russian diesel have departed the Baltic port of Primorsk for Türkiye and Brazil in recent days. Each vessel is carrying around 300,000 barrels, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters. Morocco has also resumed importing Russian diesel since the export ban was lifted.
Russia ended its self-imposed diesel export ban on 9 October after reaching a deal with US President Donald Trump to resume fuel supplies to global markets. Moscow had introduced the ban to address domestic shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Those supply problems have not been resolved, but the US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel supplies as part of the deal, allowing Moscow to prioritize export opportunities despite domestic shortages. EU and UK embargoes on Russian fuel imports remain in force.
Russian diesel exports remain below last year's levels
Russian diesel exports averaged around 345,000 barrels per day in 2026 so far, down 41% from the previous year, according to shipping data cited by Reuters. Exports had already fallen during the summer before Moscow imposed its ban.
Türkiye accounted for around 34% of Russian diesel loadings this year, followed by Brazil at 24% and Morocco at 10%, Kpler data showed.
Trump said Russia would initially export 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons afterward. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow could raise exports to as much as 3.5 million metric tons per month by the end of the year.
US seeks to ease diesel prices
The deal comes as Trump seeks to present a picture of bringing down diesel prices ahead of the US midterm elections on 3 November. Fuel prices have risen amid disruptions to global energy supplies caused by Trump's war with Iran, which has shaken oil markets and raised concerns about supply routes.
Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure for driving up energy prices, despite the broader market disruption caused by his war with Iran. The Russian diesel deal offers a way to increase global fuel supplies, but also allows Moscow to earn revenue from exports while its war against Ukraine continues.
However, the volumes from Russia initially outlined by Trump would cover only a small share of the global supply shortfall.

articles.title: Pentagon Signs Deal for Up to 25,000 APKWS Guidance Kits Annually
articles.body:
The U.S. Department of Defense has signed a framework agreement with BAE Systems to purchase up to 25,000 APKWS guidance kits annually for seven years.
The Pentagon announced the agreement on its official website.
Under the agreement, annual production could increase to 35,000 kits to meet demand from U.S.allies. However, this expansion will depend on foreign orders.
The deal still requires approval and funding from the U.S. Congress.
The total value of the planned purchases has not been disclosed. BAE Systems and the Pentagon should still negotiate a multi-year procurement contract.
APKWS (Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System) is a laser-guidance kit that converts standard unguided 70 mm Hydra70 rockets into precision-guided munitions.
The system uses semi-active laser guidance and can engage both ground and aerial targets, including drones.
In Ukraine, these rockets are used as part of VAMPIRE mobile air defense systems, whose deployment was first reported by Militarnyi in 2023.
The system includes an electro-optical detection and targeting system and a launcher that can fire four guided rockets.
In December 2025, APKWS II rockets were also spotted on a Ukrainian F-16 fighter jet, mounted in seven-shot launch pods alongside a targeting pod believed to be the Sniper XP.
This armament lets the fighter intercept drones without expending more expensive air-to-air missiles.
Militarnyi previously reported that BAE Systems had manufactured its 100,000th APKWS guidance kit. Production takes place at the company’s facilities in Hudson, New Hampshire, and Austin, Texas.

articles.title: Russian drone kills six in Kharkiv Oblast park, including mother and her 14-month-old in a stroller. Hours later, Ukraine shows photos to US senators
articles.body:
Six people were killed in a Russian strike in the settlement of Nova Vodolaha in Kharkiv Oblast, including girls aged 1 and 11. Another 15 people were injured, including seven children, Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov said on 20 October. Russian forces struck a park with a drone while families with children were there, Ukraine’s Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
Russian forces continue to attack Ukrainian cities, killing civilians and destroying civilian infrastructure. The Kharkiv Oblast Prosecutor’s Office has opened a war-crime investigation into the strike. The strike was aimed at people, Yurii Yurchenko, head of a police department in Kharkiv Oblast, said in a comment to Suspilne.
The 14-month-old girl was named Anhelina
The Russian drone circled the park several times before crashing, Yurchenko said. He said the drone struck a tree near a café, and the blast wave and shrapnel hit people at the establishment. The attack came at around 16:30, the prosecutor’s office said, adding that Russian forces had preliminarily used a Geran-3 drone.
The Russian strike killed three women, aged 28, 34 and 36, a man around 40 years old, and two girls, aged 14 months and 11 years, Syniehubov said in his statement.
The youngest girl, named Anhelina, was born in August 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Her mother, Inna, died in the hospital, he added.
Zelenskyy shows US senators photos of the aftermath the same day
Zelenskyy met with US Senators Richard Blumenthal and Thom Tillis, along with their colleagues from both parties and both chambers of Congress, according to a 19 October post on his social media accounts. During the meeting, he discussed the Russian attack in Kharkiv Oblast and showed lawmakers photographs from the scene, including one of the infant who was killed in a stroller.
“This is how Russia responds to the lifting of sanctions and the easing of pressure,” he said in the post.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine needs air defense and that no one should think about making money with Russia while it continues its war. He asked that sanctions on Russia stay in place until the killing stops, urged the US to “be strong” and apply Lindsey Graham’s law, and called on Europe to keep supporting Ukraine.

articles.title: Directed His Su-25 At An Enemy Convoy: Pilot Oleksandr Zhybrov Posthumously Awarded the Title of Hero of Ukraine
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky posthumously awarded the title of Hero of Ukraine to Lieutenant Colonel Oleksandr Zhybrov, who was killed on February 24, 2022, during an attack on a Russian military convoy in the Kherson region.
This is stated in Decree No. 1048/2026 of the President of Ukraine dated October 19, 2026.
Oleksandr Zhybrov, who commanded an aviation squadron of the 299th Tactical Aviation Brigade named after Lieutenant General Vasyl Nikiforov, was posthumously awarded the title of Hero of Ukraine along with the Order of the Golden Star.
On the first day of the full-scale Russian invasion, the lieutenant colonel organized the withdrawal of aircraft from under enemy fire and their redeployment to an operational airfield.
Oleksandr Zhybrov led the first pair of Su-25 ground-attack aircraft that set out to attack Russian columns advancing from the territory of occupied Crimea. On February 24 at 12:10 p.m., the pilot took off from the Kanatove airfield in a Su-25 ground-attack aircraft with the tail number Blue 19.
The Ukrainian pilots’ target was a convoy of Russian KrAZ-255B trucks belonging to the pontoon bridge unit near the village of Chaplynka in the Kherson region. According to the wingman’s recollection, during the attack on the convoy, they first dropped aerial bombs and then fired unguided air-to-ground missiles.
According to information from the Ukrainian State Flight Academy, after the first strike, Zhybrov noticed engineering equipment intended for building crossings over the Dnipro River and decided to launch a second attack.
During his second approach, his aircraft was hit by Russian air defense systems. Despite the damage, the pilot continued the attack and, having lost control of the attack aircraft, directed it toward the remnants of the enemy convoy.
According to the flight academy, Zhybrov then attempted to eject, but there was insufficient altitude for a safe escape. The lieutenant colonel was killed.
The body of the fallen pilot was found by local residents, who buried him in Chaplynka on March 15, 2022. In late December of that same year, the body was successfully returned to territory controlled by Ukraine. On March 11, 2023, Oleksandr Zhybrov was reburied in the Alley of Honorary Military Burials at the Far Eastern Cemetery in Kropyvnytskyi.
For his courage and self-sacrifice in defending Ukraine, the lieutenant colonel was posthumously awarded the Order of Bohdan Khmelnytsky, 3rd Class, on March 26, 2022.
In September 2026, the father of the fallen pilot donated his son’s personal belongings to the museum of the Ukrainian State Flight Academy, including his flight logbook, a flight training notebook, and a model of a Su-25 with the tail number 19.

articles.title: Pentagon deploys USS Theodore Roosevelt to Middle East as Trump weighs Iran strikes - report
articles.body:
The Pentagon is sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, two US officials confirmed to Fox News on Tuesday.
This follows a US official telling The Jerusalem Post on October 1 that the aircraft carrier and a unit of US Marines would be sent to US Central Command (CENTCOM)'s sphere of operations.
The USS Makin Island amphibious ready group also departed San Diego, carrying the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit, the Post reported at the time.
According to Fox's report, the aircraft carrier group is due to arrive in the Middle East by the end of November.
Currently, two other US aircraft carriers are deployed in the region, namely the USS George H. W. Bush, which arrived in April, and the USS George Washington, which arrived in August to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln.
However, US Naval Institute News reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt was moving to US Central Command's area of operations in order to relieve the USS George Washington.
In addition, the USS Boxer amphibious ready group is deployed in the Arabian Sea, carrying the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit, alongside the USS Portland and USS Comstock.
Additional naval deployments could provide Trump with more options if strikes on Iran ramp up after midterms
"This will provide more options for the US as President [Donald] Trump is reportedly considering ramping up strikes on Iran after the [November 3] Midterms," Fox News's Chief National Security Correspondent Jennifer Griffen wrote.
The Jerusalem Post also assessed on October 1 that, after this latest deployment, Trump will have significantly greater military capabilities and a wider range of options to act against Iran.
Meanwhile, the US military has been conducting routine troop rotations in recent weeks, and additional troops and aircraft are expected to arrive in the coming weeks as part of preparations for an escalation in the Middle East, security sources told Walla on October 4.
Some 3,000 US troops are currently stationed across Israel. Their duties include operating air defense systems, serving as pilots and support crews, and handling logistics and headquarters operations.
Amichai Stein, Idan Kweller, and Amir Bohbot contributed to this report.

articles.title: Kallas lashes out at US over Ukraine peace efforts
articles.body:
Kallas lashes out at US over Ukraine peace efforts
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has accused Washington of trying to force Ukraine to surrender to Russia, attacking President Donald Trump’s diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.
Speaking to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Tuesday, Kallas credited Europe’s military and financial backing of Kiev with prolonging the conflict and preventing Ukraine from accepting Moscow’s terms.
“American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for already almost two years, one and a half years now,” she said, as quoted by Euronews.
Moscow has cited Kiev’s aggressive posture and the hostile position of its European backers as major obstacles to a peace settlement. Ukraine has consistently rejected Russia’s conditions, insisting on joining NATO and restoring control over all territories it claims.
Kallas’ remarks came a day after US President Donald Trump said negotiations were making “great progress,” defending his decision to ease economic pressure on Russia to keep diplomacy moving.
Trump has stepped up his criticism of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, describing him as “more difficult to deal with” than Russian President Vladimir Putin. He has accused Zelensky of prolonging the conflict and taking Washington’s extensive support for granted, and has criticized Kiev’s continued attacks on Russian refineries for disrupting global diesel markets. Zelensky has said he feels betrayed by Trump.
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. On Friday, he suspended tariffs targeting China, India and other major buyers of Russian oil and gas. Trump defended the measures, saying he did not want to drive Moscow away from the negotiating table. The decisions drew criticism from European officials, with Kallas describing the diesel agreement as a “gift to Putin.”
US special envoy Steve Witkoff held talks in Oslo on Tuesday with Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner joining remotely. Witkoff is expected to travel to St. Petersburg on Wednesday for another round of discussions with Russian officials, according to Store.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Monday that Moscow “highly appreciates” Washington’s continued mediation efforts.
Russia has insisted on a long-term peace deal that addresses the root causes of the conflict, rejecting the idea of a temporary truce. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has accused Zelensky of repeatedly undermining negotiations, suggesting that any agreement acceptable to Moscow and Washington would threaten the Ukrainian leader’s hold on power.
Further financial support for Kiev has also become a source of disagreement within the EU. At Friday’s EU summit in Brussels, Zelensky demanded another €70 billion ($78.5 billion) for next year, in addition to €90 billion already pledged by the bloc to bankroll Kiev’s war effort.

articles.title: U.S. Marine Corps Establishes First Middle-Strike Missile Battalion
articles.body:
The U.S. Marine Corps has established its first battalion dedicated to conducting medium-range missile strikes.
The reorganization took place at Camp Lejeune Base in North Carolina, according to Task & Purpose.
Within the reorganization, the 1st Battalion, 10th Marine Regiment, 2nd Division, transitioned from a conventional artillery unit to a missile battalion.
The upgraded unit’s primary weapon system is NMESIS (Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System).
The NMESIS system is based on the JLTV armored vehicle and is an unmanned, remotely operated platform designed to launch two Naval Strike Missiles (NSMs).
The NSM is a low-observable, high-precision subsonic anti-ship cruise missile. It is designed to engage surface ships equipped with powerful air defense systems, as well as land targets.
The missile’s propulsion system consists of a solid-fuel booster and a Microturbo TRI 40 cruise turbojet engine. Its operational engagement range is 185–500 km, depending on the version.
The missile weighs 410 kg and is 3.9 meters long, with approximately 120 kg allocated to its penetrating blast-fragmentation warhead. Its airframe incorporates radar-absorbing materials to minimize its radar cross-section.
The NSM’s key feature is its combined guidance system. During the midcourse phase, it uses an inertial navigation system, GPS satellite navigation, and terrain-based navigation for course correction. In the terminal phase, it relies on a passive infrared seeker.
The reorganization is part of the large-scale Force Design 2030 modernization program, which aims to strengthen forward forces and expand the Corps’ anti-ship capabilities.
Other Marine Corps units had previously received individual NMESIS launchers, including the 3rd and 12th Regiments for deployment and training in the Pacific region.
The 10th Marine Regiment will retain its traditional tube artillery in another battalion, meaning the new missile systems will complement rather than fully replace the existing tube artillery.
