articles.title: One in four FSB arrest videos is staged and confessions are recorded in multiple takes after torture, Memorial finds
articles.body:
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) often stages arrests for film crews and forces suspects to record confessions multiple times, including after torture, the Memorial human rights project concluded after studying materials from 70 politically motivated criminal cases opened after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Human rights defenders found signs of staging in roughly a quarter of the examined arrest scenes, as they outline in the new report, “FSB Videos: Behind the scenes of dramatic arrests.”
According to Memorial, the FSB releases hundreds of short clips every year showing arrests, searches, and confessions. However, the real circumstances of criminal cases often differ substantially from what is shown. In some cases, detainees who are already in custody are taken outside for filming, forced to re-enact the events of their arrest, and read out confessions provided by the agency. The researchers believe the purpose of such videos is to demonstrate the FSB’s effectiveness, intimidate opponents of the Putin regime, and impose the investigators’ version on the public.
Human rights defenders also analyzed posts on the Telegram channels of the state-owned media agencies TASS and RIA Novosti. By their count, since the start of the full-scale war against Ukraine the percentage of posts mentioning the FSB has risen by a factor of between two and three. The share of FSB-related posts featuring video also doubled: from 23% in 2021 to 40% in the first half of 2026. In most cases, FSB video stories are now linked to Ukraine, primarily to accusations of terrorism and crimes against state security.
How the FSB stages arrests
One of the most vivid cases described in the study is that of Romanian national Adrian-David Kercho, who was detained in Abkhazia in November 2024 before being handed over to the FSB on Dec. 13. According to Memorial, after that Kercho was beaten, subjected to a series of back-to-back administrative arrests, and forced to confess to espionage. The security agency filmed a staged video of his arrest only on April 15, 2025, releasing it 10 days later. The date of filming was then declared the official date of Kercho’s arrest. He was subsequently sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Another example involves Yury Kayev, a defendant in the so-called “Kherson Nine” case. According to Kayev, after his actual arrest he was subjected to a week’s worth of brutal torture. Then, around a month later, security forces took him out onto a street in Kherson, handed him a bag with his personal belongings, and ordered him to walk along the pavement — warning that his arrest would be filmed. Kayev was told he should fall in such a way so as not to injure his face in front of the camera. According to Kayev, the scene was successfully shot on the first take.
The discrepancy between footage published by the FSB and the real circumstances of arrests was previously revealed by The Insider in the case of Ruslan Sidiki, who was convicted of carrying out a drone attack on the Dyagilevo military airfield and a railway bombing in Ryazan Region. The case materials studied by The Insider show that on Nov. 29, 2023, a police officer stopped Sidiki near his home in Ryazan. The officer compared the man’s face with a composite sketch and asked him to come to the police station for a conversation. Sidiki agreed. However, in the footage published by the FSB, Sidiki is shown being apprehended by armed security officers who drive up to him near a row of garages and jump out of their vehicles in order to make the arrest. Between the real arrest and the filming of the staged video, Sidiki was beaten and tortured with electric shocks. Upon admission to the pretrial detention center, numerous wounds, bruises, and hematomas were recorded.
The Insider found a similar discrepancy in July 2026, when the FSB published a video of the arrest of Anapa resident Maksim Ovchinnikov on treason charges. The Insider established his identity even though the agency had not named the detainee, and the clip itself turned out to be edited together from footage shot over the span of several months. According to an acquaintance of Ovchinnikov, the first shots date back to January 2026, when he was detained prior to his first administrative arrest. In the subsequent shots of the interrogation at the FSB directorate, green leaves are already visible on the trees, and people are wearing much lighter clothes. Ovchinnikov was first detained on Jan. 27, and on Feb. 27 FSB officers moved him from the detention facility to an unknown destination. For more than 70 days, his relatives did not know his whereabouts. In May, Ovchinnikov turned up in a pretrial detention center in Krasnodar. The FSB published the doctored arrest footage on July 4, presenting what was happening as the arrest of a man accused of treason.
Confessions after torture and in multiple takes
As the authors of the investigation note, confessions are present in almost two-thirds of the videos examined. The detainees often use official language that sounds unnatural in casual speech, reproducing the wording of specific articles from the criminal code and of investigators’ version of the events that led to their arrest. Some say that the texts of the confessions were dictated to them in advance and that the videos were redone when the result did not satisfy the FSB officers.
For example, Crimean artist Bogdan Ziza said that security forces recorded at least five versions of his apology following an anti-war demonstration. According to Ziza, the recordings were sent to superiors for approval, and the script was repeatedly changed. At one point, he was required to apologize to the Russian army, then to Vladimir Putin. When the security agents determined that he was repenting with insufficient sincerity, they beat him again. “I’m not a very good actor, and the script kept changing all the time,” Ziza said.
Denis Popovich, who was accused of plotting an assassination attempt on Metropolitan Tikhon (Shevkunov) — who is also known as Putin’s personal “confessor” — said that his confessions were recorded under torture. Speaking at Moscow’s Meshchansky District Court, Popovich said the confessions were obtained after torture with electric shocks, and that the video was recorded in several takes in order to obtain “precisely calibrated statements.”
Sometimes fragments that contradict the investigators’ version of events are removed from published recordings. For example, during a search of Nikita Ivankovich, another defendant in the case of the attempt against Metropolitan Tikhon, security forces agents found a phone and a spade. Ivankovich stated on camera that these items did not belong to him, and words made it into the original version of the clip, but some media outlets later replaced the video with an edited version that did not contain the detainee’s objections.
Videos used to pressure relatives
The researchers note that the FSB also films material not intended for public distribution. According to human rights defenders, such recordings are used to pressure detainees and their loved ones through humiliation and blackmail.
During a search, the mother of Irkutsk student Ilya Ukrainsky was shown a video of her son — beaten and crying at an unknown location. According to Memorial, security forces threatened the woman and forced her to sign documents without reading them. Ukrainsky later said that he was held for three months with no procedural status in a pretrial detention center in the Voronezh Region, where he was tortured — including by being shot in the leg during interrogations.
In another case, Chelyabinsk resident Aleksandr Novosad said in court that during a search security forces pulled his pants down, blindfolded him, wrapped him in Christmas lights, and photographed him, mocking his appearance.
The authors of the report concluded that the production of video clips has become part of the system of political repression. In their assessment, the purpose of such filming is not to document the circumstances of criminal cases but to create an atmosphere of total control, demonstrate the security forces’ power over detainees, and intimidate disloyal citizens. At the same time, the footage published by the FSB cannot be considered reliable evidence — neither of the circumstances of an arrest, nor of the timeline.

articles.title: New energy shock hits Germany
articles.body:
New energy shock hits Germany
Petroleum product prices have soared in Germany, with gasoline and diesel nearly 49% more expensive and heating oil nearly doubling over the past year, according to official figures.
The surge comes as Europe’s largest economy continues to grapple with the fallout from its break with Russian energy in 2022, now compounded by the US-Israeli war against Iran.
Prices for refined oil products jumped 51.3% year-on-year in September and 8.2% from August, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported on Tuesday. Heating oil surged 91.8%, motor fuels rose 48.6%, and naphtha, used in chemical manufacturing, climbed 53.8%.
The figures reflect producer prices rather than those paid by consumers at the pump.
The shock spread across the energy sector. Producer energy prices rose 14.9% year-on-year, with natural gas distribution costs up 15% and electricity 8.2%.
Germany’s crude oil import bill also surged despite slightly lower purchases. In the first eight months of 2026, the cost jumped 21.7% to €30 billion ($33.6 billion), while volumes fell 0.6% to 49.1 million tons. Destatis attributed the increase to higher crude oil prices amid the Middle East conflict.
The pressure has spread across German industry. Overall producer prices rose 6.7% year-on-year in September, the sharpest increase since March 2023. Manufacturing materials and components became 6.4% more expensive, while machinery and equipment rose 2.4%. Excluding energy, producer prices were up 3.2%.
The Iran war has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, driving up energy prices worldwide. Brent crude topped $111 a barrel on Tuesday, a five-month high, while US benchmark WTI exceeded $104.
Although Gulf crude oil shipments have reportedly recovered to around 80% of pre-war levels, new Iranian attacks on vessels have kept markets on edge. Escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis has added pressure, with strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure and renewed clashes near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait threatening another key shipping route linking the Red Sea to global markets.
Germany’s energy troubles, however, predate the Middle East crisis. The country has faced high costs since abandoning cheap Russian energy following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, forcing energy-intensive manufacturers to seek more expensive alternatives.
Before the break, Russia supplied 55% of Germany’s natural gas imports. Direct imports from Russia have since fallen to zero, with Germany reportedly paying five times as much for gas. Norway (44%), the Netherlands (24%), and Belgium (21%) have become its main suppliers, with US liquefied natural gas (LNG) accounting for much of the remainder.
Berlin has spent around €50 billion to cushion the price shock since cutting Russian gas imports, German media reported last month. Yet the economy remains sluggish, with corporate insolvencies hitting a 13-year high in the first half of 2026. Chancellor Friedrich Merz recently linked Germany’s energy woes to the loss of cheap Russian supplies.
Meanwhile, Berlin committed €96 billion in Ukraine-related support, launched a €100 billion rearmament drive, and pledged to raise core defense spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2029.
Amid criticism that increased military spending is at the expense of domestic needs, Merz’s approval rating sank to a record-low 10% in a poll in October. His Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has suffered major electoral setbacks against the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has overtaken the CDU-led bloc in national polling. The AfD has called for Russian gas imports to be restored.
Moscow has long argued that Western energy sanctions are counterproductive, redirecting Russian exports while forcing Europeans to pay more for alternative supplies. Russia has offered to cover shortages and resume deliveries, but says its proposals have gone unanswered.

articles.title: Europe is preparing for direct talks with Putin, FT reports. One possible proposal: Russia gets Donbas, Ukraine gets NATO membership.
articles.body:
Europe is preparing for direct talks with Putin, FT reports. One possible proposal: Russia gets Donbas, Ukraine gets NATO membership.
European leaders are rethinking their approach to the Kremlin, Financial Times foreign affairs columnist Gideon Rachman writes. More politicians in the European Union now agree that negotiations with Vladimir Putin should not remain the exclusive prerogative of the United States. European countries could soon open their own talks with the Kremlin. Channels of communication are already in place, he says.
EU policy toward Russia has rested on two main pillars until now: support for Ukraine and sanctions. European leaders have tried to shape the negotiations by influencing Donald Trump’s position, but those efforts are growing less effective. Europe also fears Trump is more interested in business deals with Moscow than in security issues.
In any direct talks, Putin could be offered two options for ending the war, Rachman writes: freezing the conflict along the front line in exchange for a guarantee that Ukraine will not join NATO, or ceding all of the Donbas to Moscow’s control, after which Kyiv could join the alliance.
Meanwhile, relations between Kyiv and Washington are going through a new crisis, triggered by an energy crisis and Trump’s push to lower diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections to Congress.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries and declare an energy truce. After diplomatic failure, he struck a deal with Moscow on diesel supplies. Volodymyr Zelensky said the United States had “chosen the side” of Russia. Trump responded that it was easier for him to reach an agreement with Putin than with Zelensky, adding that Ukraine needs to hold elections.
Relations between the two leaders are at their “lowest point” since the clash in the Oval Office in 2025, the WSJ writes. The latest exchange took place a day earlier: Trump accused Zelensky of not wanting to end the war, while Zelensky said Ukraine is being pressured to capitulate.
Amid this, U.S. Vice President JD Vance has spoken out against Ukraine joining NATO: “We don’t have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They’re not in NATO. I don’t think that they should be in NATO,” he said. Vance also refused to call Kyiv an ally of Washington, saying they have “divergent interests from time to time.”
War in photographs. Komyshuvakha.
Residents of Komyshuvakha, a front-line village in the Zaporizhzhia region, are being evacuated because of the threat of Russian drone strikes. These photos were taken October 19, 2026.

The source told Tasnim that Ukraine has deployed drone units—equipped with micro-drones—across several countries in the region (surrounding Iran).
The source added that Ukraine’s activities include the establishment of an operational network for micro-drones in the region.
Noting that the identities of the host nations—which are harboring these Ukrainian forces and drones—are being withheld for now but will be disclosed at an appropriate time, the source stated that Ukrainian operatives have deployed thousands of micro-drones within the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.
The security source emphasized that Tehran views this move by Ukraine as part of a broader campaign of hostile actions by Europe and NATO against Iran, and is currently considering an appropriate response.
Describing these conspiratorial moves as a “failed attempt” and “a scandal” for Ukraine, the source said that Tehran is fully aware of—and closely monitoring—Kiev’s hostile activities.
Referring to a past incident in which Ukraine targeted an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea—an act of hostility to which Iran showed restraint—the source said Iran will not allow Europe or Ukraine or give them the opportunity to advance anti-Iranian agendas.
These remarks come amid reports that Ukraine has participated in anti-Iranian activities—especially regarding drone-related support for parties involved in the 40-day US-Israeli aggression against Iran—including by providing assistance to nations in the Persian Gulf that host US military bases. There have previously been discussions regarding the presence of Ukrainian forces in West Asia—aimed at carrying out acts of sabotage and training terrorists in the use of drones—leading analysts to describe the country as a new operational arm for NATO in the region.
In this context, in the summer of 2025, the police in Sulaymaniyah, northern Iraq, announced the arrest of three Ukrainians who were overseeing the training of a local group in the use of small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
The Sulaymaniyah police added that the training was intended to facilitate assassination operations, funded and supervised by a terrorist group operating in northern Iraq.
This is not the first time that Ukrainian-linked operatives have been implicated in events across the Middle East. Currently, personnel from Ukraine’s security apparatus are operating as mercenaries in various regions, receiving payment from the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Zionist regime.
The first instance of Ukrainians engaging in sabotage in this region dates back to the attack on a graduation ceremony at the military academy in Homs, Syria. At the time, Russian sources reported that the operation was directed by Ukrainian operatives.
The drone attack in Homs in October 2023 resulted in at least 100 deaths—many of whom were family members of the young Syrian officers who were killed in the strike.

articles.title: Netanyahu, Hegseth hold 'secret' meeting at south Israel airbase
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Netanyahu, Hegseth hold 'secret' meeting at southern Israel airbase
An unannounced meeting was held between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in southern Israel on Monday, US news site Axios reported.
The meeting took place at Ovda airbase in the Negev desert, where US fighter jets and refuelling aircraft are stationed, two sources familiar with the matter told Axios.
Hegseth has since confirmed that the secret trip took place. Other than saying he had met with US troops, he gave no further details.
"It was an honour to visit our warfighters in @CENTCOM today. The best of our country, on a historic mission. Godspeed," he wrote on X.
Netanyahu flew to the airbase from Israel’s main airport, Ben Gurion, by private plane rather than helicopter, which Israeli news outlet Ynet described as unusual. Ynet also said the meeting was "unusually" long.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and National Security Adviser Shmuel Ben-Ezra also attended the meeting, according to Axios and Israel’s Channel 12.
Earlier reports in Israeli media suggested that officials from the United Arab Emirates were also present, but Israeli news outlet i24NEWS later reported that no Emirati officials had attended.
Reports of Hegseth’s trip emerged a day after US President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu in Israel’s 27 October election. The visit also comes amid heightened US-Israel tensions with Iran and growing concerns about a possible resumption of war.
The US and Israel began striking Iran on 28 February, immediately drawing much of the region into a wider conflict that has left thousands of people dead and rattled the global economy amid disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab.
Oil- and gas-rich Gulf states have come under repeated Iranian attack. The ongoing conflict between Yemen’s Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia has become another major front in the wider war.
On Monday, senior sources familiar with mediation efforts told The New Arab that a breakthrough in US-Iran talks was expected to be announced this week, as Qatar and Pakistan continued diplomatic efforts to prevent a renewed war. However, the prospect of an agreement remained highly uncertain, with Tehran refusing to make concessions on its nuclear programme and support for its allied groups across the region.
Tehran has warned that it would retaliate forcefully if Washington and Tel Aviv resumed their attacks.
Earlier this month, Hegseth told reporters: "Iran will never, under any circumstances, possess a nuclear weapon. President Trump is absolutely determined and resolved to ensure they do not obtain one. They will not get it."
He warned that Iran had the option of complying with US demands or, as he put it, "learning the hard way."

articles.title: Mother of all bombs or father of all missiles?
articles.body:
Mother of all bombs or father of all missiles?
In a note, Etemad examined US rhetoric about using the “Mother of All Bombs” and Iran’s response that it could employ the “Father of All Missiles.” The paper argued that Iran’s statements do not necessarily mean such bombs would be ineffective, nor that Tehran has publicly revealed the nature or scope of any potential response. Political declarations, deterrent warnings, and military operational plans are three distinct matters.
The verbal clash between the “Mother of All Bombs and the Father of All Missiles” reflects a battle of narratives more than a definitive answer to a military question. Washington seeks to intimidate through displays of destructive power, while Tehran emphasizes its retaliatory capabilities and the costs of any attack. Ultimately, the impact of either narrative will depend not on the names of bombs and missiles but on real military capabilities, political decisions, and the consequences of any confrontation.
Khorasan: Iran has achieved many of its war objectives
Khorasan argued that Iran has already achieved many of its goals in the conflict. According to the paper, many of the developments currently unfolding in Europe are a result of Iran’s actions. While Western governments had intended to dedicate significant financial resources to supporting their populations, they have instead been forced to return to older policies to manage the economic consequences of the war. This has led to growing public dissatisfaction and notable social reactions. The newspaper claimed that Iran has already attained a large portion of its objectives: it succeeded in limiting the conflict from a national to a regional level, forcing its foes to operate under those constraints. It also asserted that Iran overcame infrastructure-focused warfare, severely suppressed enemy agents within the country, and maintained overall domestic stability by preventing major shortages and deep economic stagnation.
Ettelaat: Which side will compromise, Iran or the US?
Ettelaat discussed the lack of progress in ongoing negotiations between Iran and the United States, citing former Minister of Culture and Islamic Guidance Ali Jannati. He argued that diplomacy has not failed, because opportunities for negotiation remain available even under the most difficult circumstances. Over the past month, Qatari mediators have reportedly conveyed Iranian proposals to the United States and delivered Washington’s responses back to Tehran. According to Jannati, the talks have stalled because Iran proposed seven principles as the basis for negotiations and the United States broadly accepted the framework but strongly disagreed over the sequence in which the provisions should be implemented. Washington wants the nuclear issue to be addressed first, whereas Tehran views it as the final matter for discussion. He suggested that both sides continue to insist on their positions and that little progress is likely unless one party shows flexibility and makes concessions. Otherwise, he warned, the possibility of renewed war remains.
Vatan-e-Emrooz: France bowed to Hormuz
Vatan-e-Emrooz analyzed protests in France and comments made by President Macron. According to the paper, Macron acknowledged in a televised address that French citizens had reason to be upset about rising fuel prices linked to developments in the Persian Gulf. The newspaper noted that Macron had previously stated that France was living with the consequences of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. It linked current economic pressures to events eight months earlier, when US and Israeli attacks on Iran led to the closure of the strategic waterway. The paper argued that the disruption of oil shipments through Hormuz triggered increases in fuel costs, inflation, and living expenses worldwide. It contended that these economic effects have fueled ongoing protests in France, which began in mid-September over shortages of teachers and inadequate school facilities but have continued for more than a month due to broader concerns about the cost of living.
Shargh: Repeated US threats aim to weaken social resilience
In an interview with Shargh, Seyed Jalil Mirmohammadi Meybodi, a member of the Iranian Parliament’s Industries and Mines Committee, discussed the main source of “psychological warfare” against Iran by the Trump administration. He argued that it originates from US policy and Washington’s extensive media capabilities. Psychological warfare is one of America’s principal tools in its confrontation with Iran, and Tehran faces an enemy that controls powerful global media networks. He claimed that the United States has failed to achieve its objectives and has therefore resorted to new threats and attempts to project victory. He said that Donald Trump continually seeks to portray himself as victorious and might use a major military action, such as a large-scale bombing campaign, to claim success. Meybodi also argued that any new military action against Iran would be met with a reciprocal response. In his view, frequent public discussion of war often makes actual conflict less likely, and recurring threats may be intended more to influence Iran’s political and psychological calculations than to signal an imminent military operation.

articles.title: Air Force’s Top Planner Lays Out Vision for Fighter Fleet Mix by 2035
articles.body:
Roughly two of every five fighters in the Air Force fleet could be F-35As by 2035, according to a new fighter force structure report the service submitted to Congress on Oct. 16.
Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, revealed the new estimate during an Oct. 20 media roundtable at the Pentagon as he explained the report’s estimates of the future force’s mix of different types of fighters.
The Air Force did not provide a full copy of the report to reporters.
About 40 percent of the fleet could be F-35s, Tabor said. Another 20 percent would be a combination of F-22 Raptors and F-47s as the sixth-generation fighter replaces the Raptor. The Air Force built 186 operational F-22s, and Tabor said the Air Force still plans to replace them with roughly an equivalent number of F-47s. The remaining 40 percent of the fleet would likely be split evenly between F-15 Eagle variants and F-16 Fighting Falcons, Tabor said.

Currently, the fighter fleet—not counting A-10s—is split roughly 45 percent F-16s, 30 percent F-35s, 15 percent F-15s, and 10 percent F-22s.
Beyond the mix of the fighters, the force structure report also provides a new estimate of the total number of fighters the Air Force says it will need in the years to come: 1,509 combat-coded aircraft by 2035.
That’s up from the 1,271 the service estimated it would have in 2026 and the 1,369 combat-coded fighters it was shooting for by 2030 in last year’s report, Tabor said. The additional 140 jets would be a mixture of F-35s, F-15EXs, and F-47s.
The data used for the previous report was “pretty old,” Tabor said, so the service’s researchers set out to compile fresher and more accurate information. This analysis was going on before combat operations against Iran broke out earlier this year, he said, and was not driven by the war.
The Air Force’s analysis was based on geographic combatant commanders’ reported requirements to achieve their goals at “medium risk,” Tabor said, and he cautioned that is based on their subjective assessments of what they will need—and will likely change in the future.
“Certainly, world events and changing requirements in the combatant commands will change that number,” Tabor said. “Capabilities that we bring on to platforms will change the number, and I think really importantly, technology will change the number.”
Getting to the new 2035 goal depends on two key factors falling into place, Tabor said. First, Congress will need to provide the funds the Air Force needs to buy the jets. And the defense industrial base—in particular, prime contractors Lockheed Martin and Boeing—must produce enough aircraft in time.
Top Air Force officials have for years said the service needs to buy 72 new fighters each year to replace its older, retiring jets and modernize the fleet. The fiscal 2027 budget request doesn’t reach that level, proposing 38 new F-35s and 24 F-15EXs for a total of 62. Tabor said those purchases can “ramp over time” to hit the numbers the Air Force needs.
“The question is, can industry produce at those levels?” Tabor said. “They’ve assured us that they can, and we believe them, but we also actually need to see it manifest.”
Right now, 2027’s funding levels remain a big question mark. The administration’s strategy for funding the Pentagon this year relies on a budget reconciliation bill to add additional funding priorities on top of the proposed “base” appropriations.
The Air Force’s proposed budget counted on $2.34 billion coming through reconciliation to pay for 14 of those 38 new F-35s. If reconciliation doesn’t pass, Tabor said, the Air Force is not out of options. It could try to find money in the base budget to pay for more F-35s, he said—though that would require pulling billions from other critical programs.
“We just lose 14 times [an] F-35’s worth of other capabilities that we were planning on,” Tabor said.
Or, he said, the purchases could be pushed out to 2028, which would further put the Air Force behind on reaching its fighter fleet goals.
“It is really imperative that we get the resourcing we need in order to modernize the Air Force the way we want it to be,” Tabor said. “We need it all.”
In the meantime, the clock is ticking on large portions of the Air Force’s fleet such as older F-15s and F-16s, which are aging and reaching the end of their lifespans.
The Air Force is considering buying a new version of the F-16, which is tentatively being referred to as the F-16G. But the Air Force has not yet made any decision on that, Tabor said, “and we’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately.” That decision likely won’t be made as part of the 2028 budgeting process, he said, but perhaps the years that follow.
Older F-16s will reach the end of their lifespans in the mid-2030s, Tabor said, and “we are very conscious of that.” The simple—“and maybe the lazy”—way to approach that problem, Tabor said, is to automatically replace them with new F-16s. But that might not be the best strategy, he said.
“There is a spectrum of capability that we might want to replace the F-16s with,” he said. “It’s not urgent, frankly. What we don’t want to get to is a point where it is urgent, and we haven’t done the homework and decided ‘hey, this is really the right place to be.’ We do have time to churn through that and make sure that we have a good option going forward.”
One advantage to buying more F-16s, which Lockheed Martin now builds in Greenville, S.C., is that “it’s practically a ready-made aircraft,” Tabor said—if the Air Force wants to stick with the same type of capabilities.
Another potential wrinkle is the Pentagon’s push to expand its multiyear procurement authorities. The Air Force is eyeing such agreements for the F-35 and F-15EX, though its request is pending before Congress. More multiyear procurement deals will help provide industry more financial stability, Tabor said, which could make it easier for them to expand and stabilize production of fighters.
But while the Air Force is rapidly preparing to add hundreds of autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft to its fleet—the goal is 500 airframes by 2032—Tabor said they’re not yet changing the service’s calculus on what fighter force it will need in the future.
“CCA is very much a reality,” Tabor said. “It is going to be a part of our future, and there is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters. That’s not the CCA that we have right now, but it is advancing very, very rapidly. We’re confident that it will play a major role in future versions of the fighter force structure report.”

articles.title: Rubio insists delays in interceptor deliveries to Kyiv are not deliberate
articles.body:
Rubio insists delays in interceptor deliveries to Kyiv are not deliberate
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio insists that "nothing has changed" regarding the supply of American weapons to Ukraine under the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme.
Source: Rubio during his visit to India, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Rubio acknowledged that deliveries of interceptor missiles to Ukraine may be delayed because many US allies are seeking the same weapons. However, he said the PURL programme continues to operate as before and that the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Quote: "So, let me clear those up. And as I did in my conversation with him [President Volodymyr Zelenskyy – ed.], number one is the Department of War, everything they've been doing with Ukraine remains the same. That has not changed. Nothing has changed… The second is intelligence sharing. The president [Donald Trump – ed.] made it very clear. He's ordered no such changes. So, none of that has changed."
Details: Rubio noted that interceptor missiles remain the most sought-after type of weaponry in the world, which could lead to delays in deliveries.
Quote: "Every country in the world would like interceptors. And many parts of the world are asking for that. It's probably the most in-demand product right now in the defence field. So when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own needs too…
There is nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine. It's simply a balance between our obligations to other partners and, frankly, our own standards and requirements for our own facilities as well."
Details: Rubio stressed that any delays in the supply of American weapons to Ukraine are not politically motivated.
"I think the important takeaway for you is that there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he added.
Background:
- On 19 October, Zelenskyy said the US Department of War is delaying the delivery of resources Ukraine needs.
- The president has also accused the US of trying to pressure Kyiv into capitulating to Russia.

articles.title: Canada can help Seoul counter North Korea’s new ‘ways of war’: Military chief
articles.body:
Canada’s Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan speaks during an interview with NK News at the Canadian Embassy in Seoul on Oct. 16, 2026. | Image: NK News
Canada can share lessons from training Ukrainian forces to help South Korea learn how to defeat the new “ways of war” that North Korea is mastering through Russia’s war, Canada’s top military commander told NK News.
Gen. Jennie Carignan, Canada’s chief of the defense staff, said in an exclusive interview in Seoul that North Korea’s growing combat experience is a concern for Canada and its allies. She pointed to drones and automated systems as a natural area for cooperation, and said both militaries must stay agile because the next war will not look exactly like the one in Ukraine.
Joon Ha Park is a correspondent at Korea Risk Group. He has previously written on issues related to the two Koreas at The Peninsula Report, and appeared on ABC News Australia, Deutsche Welle and Monocle Radio. He specializes in offering in-depth analyses of South Korea’s defense policy, security relations and domestic politics for Korea Pro.

Interceptors, ballistic missile warnings and Starlink: Zelenskyy details call with Rubio
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has spoken with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio about interceptors for ballistic missiles, early warning of Russian missile attacks and restoring Starlink/Starshield services.

articles.title: Witkoff to visit St. Petersburg after Zelensky talks, Norway's PM says
articles.body:
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian officials in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21 to discuss European and U.S. proposals for peace in Ukraine, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said.
This will "possibly pave the way for a meeting at leaders' level," Store said at a press conference in Oslo on Oct. 20 after talks with Witkoff and President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The officials, as well as Finnish President Alexander Stubb, met in Norway in a precarious moment for Ukraine, with Russia escalating attacks against energy infrastructure.
Meanwhile, Kyiv's ties with Washington are sharply deteriorating amid concerns that the U.S. could be withholding the delivery of Patriot air-defense missiles funded by Ukraine's allies, as well as other support.
read also
"We have some clear ideas on how to get to peace. And we are united with our European partners in this effort, and we want the Americans to take these ideas to the Russians," Zelensky said at the press conference.
"One of the important ideas is to move to a trilateral meeting of the leaders, to address the issues that only the leaders can do."
Witkoff will also present to the Russian side proposals on Article 5-like post-war security guarantees for Ukraine, which were discussed in Oslo, Zelensky said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has long evaded a meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief reportedly pushes to meet U.S. President Donald Trump in China next month to secure a favorable peace deal, without Ukraine at the table.
"We discussed and found key elements on security, and we discussed and found key elements on the economy," Stubb commented on the latest talks, saying that proposals have been developed by European, Ukrainian, and U.S. officials.
The Finnish president remarked that despite "a lot of noise in the public space," negotiations are advancing well "on the technical level."
Jared Kushner joined the talks in Oslo online, and officials are also expected to hold discussions with national security advisors from European countries.
Witkoff was not present at the final press conference. When asked about his absence by a reporter, Store said, "This is a press conference among political leaders."
The New York Times reported earlier that Witkoff would meet Putin while in Russia, possibly to discuss the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 72-year-old American citizen who was reportedly serving with a Ukrainian territorial defense unit in Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, when Russian forces detained him in 2022.
More than a year and a half of U.S.-led peace efforts have failed to make headway as Moscow continues to demand that Ukraine cede Donbas, a strategically vital region in Ukraine's east that Russian forces were unable to take fully by force.
The peace push has now been further hampered by a sharp deterioration in Ukraine-U.S. relations, following the unexpected announcement of a U.S.-Russia diesel deal on Oct. 9.
Since then, Zelensky and Trump have exchanged sharp public criticism. Trump said his Ukrainian counterpart "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
Trump has also refused to condemn the Kremlin over its escalating attacks on Ukraine, including strikes on the country's already vulnerable energy infrastructure.
Zelensky, meanwhile, warned in an interview with NBC News that siding with Putin would be a "historic mistake."

articles.title: Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest
articles.body:
Why Rubio is visiting Reliance’s oil refinery in India, the world’s largest
Reliance is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers and contain oil prices amid the war on Iran with a crucial midterm election looming.
New Delhi, India — United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has arrived in India for a two-day visit, during which he is set to tour the Jamnagar refinery complex in Gujarat, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, a major player in global oil markets.
Reliance’s crude refinery in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state is the world’s largest single-site refinery. In many ways, Reliance Industries’ businesses sit at the crossroads of the ongoing global energy crisis.
The conglomerate is central to Washington’s efforts to punish Russian energy buyers, while also trying to contain oil prices amid the war on Iran, on top of rising diesel costs in the US, where a crucial midterm election looms. Reliance has also only recently committed to a major investment in the US, which President Donald Trump’s administration has cited as an example of its successes in luring global capital.
Rubio is skipping the capital, New Delhi, at a time when the US-India bilateral relationship has been rocky, strained by a string of friction points — and an elusive trade deal.
So why is the top US diplomat visiting the world’s largest single-site oil refinery?
Where is Rubio visiting?
After meetings in Mumbai, India’s financial hub in the western state of Maharashtra, Rubio will fly to Jamnagar in neighbouring Gujarat, near the Gulf of Kutch. Jamnagar opens into the Arabian Sea and is home to Reliance Industries’ refining complex, a major hub for crude processing and fuel exports, which processes 1.4 million barrels per day (bpd).
Rubio had visited India earlier this year too, but this trip “is a little more business-focused”, the US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, told reporters last week. A readout from Rubio’s office noted that he would “meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation”.
“[At Jamnagar] he will meet some of the folks at Reliance,” Gor said.
What’s in Jamnagar?
The world’s largest single-site oil-refining complex has a combined crude-processing capacity of 1.4 million bpd. That is nearly 1.5 percent of global refining capacity, according to the company.
The complex comprises two refineries: the original facility, commissioned in 1999 with a capacity of 660,000bpd, and a second, export-oriented refinery commissioned in 2008, adding 580,000bpd, which operates in a special economic zone.
Jamnagar imports crude from international suppliers and exports refined products to global markets. The refinery can process heavy, sulphur-rich crude that many facilities cannot handle efficiently, converting oil into higher-value products.
Reliance said last month that the complex has processed more than 216 crude grades, claiming to be “perhaps the only refinery to achieve this feat”.
The Jamnagar refinery’s capacity is also driving a sharp revival in imports of Venezuelan crude — taken over by the US earlier this year after abducting then-President Nicolas Maduro — as Washington seeks to reshape global oil trade.
Reliance is expected to account for roughly 350,000bpd to 370,000bpd of the October intake, according to estimates from analytics firm Kpler. “We will talk with Reliance about refining more Venezuelan crude,” Rubio told reporters in brief remarks on Tuesday.
Why is the refinery significant for global energy supplies?
Reliance is a central player in keeping global oil markets stable, as one of the world’s biggest suppliers of refined petroleum products. In September, for instance, six of the seven large cargo ships that docked at European Union ports carrying oil products were bearing Reliance goods.
Reliance’s biggest export is diesel, which Trump has been particularly worried about, with prices reaching historic highs in the US ahead of midterm elections early next month.
Though the data on exports by category is not public, an analysis by the Reuters news agency from trade sources noted that Reliance Industries exported 21.66 million tonnes of refined petroleum products in the first half of 2025 from Jamnagar. Diesel accounted for the largest share at 9.81 million tonnes, followed by petrol at 6.14 million tonnes and jet fuel at 2.06 million tonnes.
Europe accounted for the biggest share of the company’s exports, making up 28 percent of Reliance’s refined products during the period. Buyers include BP, ExxonMobil, Glencore, Vitol and Trafigura.
The Jamnagar refinery also shipped about $143m worth of oil products to the US last month, according to data cited by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a think tank in Finland.
CREA noted in its report that the EU’s ban on importing petroleum products made from Russian crude from January 2026 does not adequately prevent products from refineries in third countries from entering Europe when those refineries also process Russian crude. The Jamnagar refinery is a prime example of that loophole.
Rubio’s visit to the refinery also comes as Trump faces his worst approval ratings amid inflation and rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm election in November. Just about 31 percent of Americans are happy with Trump’s performance – the lowest-ever number in his two terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey.
The Trump administration has also reportedly been pushing Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop strikes on Russian energy facilities, which have rattled the global fuel markets.
Why the refinery is important for the Russia-Ukraine war
Reliance is also a critical actor in US efforts to influence how much oil Russia sells.
Since the start of Russia’s full-fledged war on Ukraine in February 2022, India has emerged as the second-largest buyer of Russian oil after China. And Reliance is driving that surge in imports. While only 3 percent of its oil was sourced from Russia before 2022, that share rose to 50 percent by 2025.
So when Trump imposed an additional 25 percent tariff on Indian goods in August 2025 to punish New Delhi for the purchase of Russian oil, Reliance was directly affected. It cut back on Russian crude imports significantly in subsequent months, but it still made up a third of the oil processed by Jamnagar’s refinery during the July-September 2026 quarter.
That was under threat when the Trump administration appeared poised to impose a 100 percent tariff on Indian goods because of continued Russian oil imports, under a new law passed last month.
But Trump has since suspended those proposed tariffs, easing concerns for India and Reliance.
Rubio has said India has been diversifying its import mix away from Russian crude, even as it still buys millions of barrels of Russian oil every day. “You’ve got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it’s hard to pivot from one day to the next,” Rubio said on Sunday.
“But they’re also an important ally and partner of the United States.”
Is Reliance also investing in the US?
Yes, India’s richest man, Mukesh Ambani, the chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries, is investing in the US, primarily through energy-related projects.
It is backing America First Refining’s planned oil refinery at the Port of Brownsville in Texas, also the first major US refinery in about 50 years, announced by Trump in March.
The refinery is expected to cost $3bn to $4bn and process about 60 million barrels of US crude annually. Reliance has signed a 20-year agreement to buy a large share of the facility’s output, with operations expected to start around 2029.
In November 2024, Reliance’s US subsidiary also acquired a 21 percent stake in helium explorer Wavetech Helium for $12m as part of its low-carbon energy strategy.
Last month, Trump announced that India’s Essar Group — an oil major with knee-deep ties to Russia — is planning an $18bn integrated steel investment in the US through its subsidiary, Mesabi Metallics.
Didn’t Trump’s ally just lock horns with Ambani?
Despite Reliance’s investments in the US and Rubio’s upcoming visit to the Jamnagar facility, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man who is also a key Trump ally, recently hit out at Ambani.
His Starlink space telecommunications firm has struggled for years to secure a licence to operate in India.
In a series of X posts recently, Musk accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government of stalling Starlink’s entry to favour market leader Ambani’s telecom firm, Jio. Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Starlink, Musk wrote, was being blocked by “oligarchs” protecting their “monopolistic chokehold” on Indians.
In a statement issued on X, Reliance said it has “never feared competition” and has “grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international”.

articles.title: Russia’s Rubicon hunts Ukrainian drone pilots. In Vivaldi, it became the target, and its morale fell sharply, says the Ukrainian general
articles.body:
Russia’s Rubicon drone unit, which is sent to hunt Ukrainian drone pilots, was not used to being hunted itself, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi told journalists on 19 October. He was summing up Operation Vivaldi, which his Third Army Corps fought in northern Donetsk Oblast from May to mid-October. Once its pilots realized they were being killed, Rubicon’s morale dropped sharply, he said.
Russia has fought for 12 years to take all of Donetsk Oblast, and Sloviansk and Kramatorsk anchor the fortress belt of cities Ukraine still holds there. Vivaldi retook 277 km² in northern Donetsk Oblast. Biletskyi says it destroyed Russia’s bridgehead on the Chornyi Zherebets River and forced Moscow to drop its plan to bypass Lyman from the north and encircle the two cities. On that front, the Third Corps had flagged Rubicon, Russia’s elite drone unit, as a threat.
Hunting the hunters
Once a Rubicon position was found, the Third Assault Brigade and the KRAKEN drone regiment committed any number of FPV and bomber drones to destroy its crews, Biletskyi said.
The brigade’s commander, Yaroslav Levenets, said his troops prepared for Rubicon’s arrival and concentrated on killing its pilots. He gave no details.
“Not stable in defense,” Levenets said of Rubicon’s troops.
They dislike sitting in trenches, he said, and under pressure they grow nervous and change positions.
Named for four seasons
Biletskyi said the name was chosen at the very start of planning, in winter 2025–2026, many months before the operation began. The original plan had four stages, one for each season, and later grew to slightly more, ArmyInform reported.
When he first unveiled the operation in September, he put it this way:
“Vivaldi, as is known, has four seasons. And this is only the first one.”
He credited two planners, known by the call signs Yurist and Leshyi. Leshyi, an assault soldier wounded seven times who later moved to staff work, was killed. Yurist was seriously wounded.
Ukraine blocks Russia from outflanking its fortress cities in Donbas, retaking 277 square kilometers and hitting 8,000 Russian troops
A new hand at the Third Corps
Major Dmytro Rohoziuk is now acting commander of the Third Army Corps, the corps press service said on 20 October. The press service said the move is not a transfer, and Biletskyi keeps his formal post as corps commander while he leads the “Center” grouping of the Third, 11th, and 19th corps.
Rohoziuk took over the 60th Mechanized Brigade in October 2025. Its previous commander was arrested in January after the State Bureau of Investigation accused him of embezzling about $1 million in weapons procurement. The brigade fought in all four phases of Vivaldi and retook Kolodiazi without street fighting.
Biletskyi also declined command of the Ground Forces, which oversee mobilization.
“There’s no point taking on something you don’t truly believe you can improve,” he said.
Biletskyi’s count
Russian losses in Vivaldi topped 8,000 troops, and about 270 Russian soldiers were taken prisoner, Biletskyi said. More than 20 officers surrendered, including a chief of staff and three company commanders.
The territory matters less than disrupting Russia’s strategic plan, he said. Russian forces still press toward Dobropillia, where Ukraine is counterattacking.

- Ukraine is saving Donetsk Oblast with world’s first-of-its-kind operation: Vivaldi counteroffensive drops robots directly from heavy bombers 10 kilometers behind Russian lines
- New Vivaldi tactic: Ukraine’s ground robots, each carrying two Bullspike grenade launchers, attack Russian positions and then detonate inside their shelters

articles.title: Exclusive: Mediators submit new peace proposal to Iran, US
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Mediators submit new peace proposal to Iran, US
Qatari and Pakistani officials submitted a new peace proposal to Iran and the US on Tuesday in a bid to prevent further escalation in the Middle East war, sources familiar with the mediation efforts told The New Arab.
The people described the plan as a "middle-ground proposal" that partially meets both sides' demands over Iran's nuclear programme and the release of Tehran's frozen assets. It has received positive responses from both Washington and Tehran, they said.
Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir delivered the proposal to Iranian officials in Tehran on Tuesday, according to the sources, who spoke to TNA on condition of anonymity.
Neither side has shown willingness to compromise over their demands, with the US still insisting Tehran must dismantle its nuclear programme and Iran demanding the immediate release of all its assets frozen abroad.
After agreeing to a temporary ceasefire in June, the two sides were supposed to begin negotiating a comprehensive peace deal covering the nuclear programme and Iran's frozen assets.
But since that truce fell apart the following month, no further negotiations have been held. Tensions have instead ratcheted up further in recent days, with Iran increasing its attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Trump threatening to return to war after November's midterm elections.
The sources said that the latest proposal aims to extract minor concessions from both sides in a bid to build confidence for new talks. Under the deal, Iran would agree to a secret, unannounced visit by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to inspect its nuclear sites. In return, the US would allow Tehran to receive the interest generated on its $6 billion of frozen assets held in Qatar.
On Monday, sources familiar with the negotiations told The New Arab that a breakthrough could be announced later this week.
The sources, who also requested anonymity, said efforts were continuing to narrow the differences between the two sides and encourage them to make mutual concessions to prevent the war from resuming.
Qatar and Pakistan are pursuing joint mediation efforts aimed at ending the seven-month regional war. Both countries mediated June's memorandum of understanding that briefly brought the conflict to a halt.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Tuesday that Iranian officials would discuss the peace negotiations with Munir.
Munir's visit comes amid mounting tensions over Iran's nuclear programme, the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz and US demands for Tehran to curb its enrichment capabilities.
President Trump and other US officials have issued new threats to restart the war if Iran does not back down, while Iranian officials have said they are ready for renewed conflict. On Saturday, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth warned that Iran would face "destruction" unless it abandoned its nuclear ambitions.
The mediation efforts also coincide with intensifying regional and international diplomatic activity, including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s visit to Tehran on Monday.

articles.title: Exclusive: Iraq imposes restrictions on Houthis’ Baghdad office
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraq imposes restrictions on Houthis’ Baghdad office
Iraq has imposed restrictions on representatives of Yemen’s Houthi group in Baghdad, banning them from political and media activities amid regional tensions and efforts to strengthen ties with Saudi Arabia, sources have told The New Arab (TNA).
Houthi leaders and officials in Iraq have been instructed not to conduct any media or political “activities” from Iraqi territory, an Iraqi official who requested anonymity told TNA.
A senior official in the office of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the directive imposed a comprehensive ban on members of the group in Iraq holding meetings, organising press conferences and seminars, or moving outside the limits permitted under the country’s residency laws.
Since 2018, the Houthis have operated an office in Baghdad’s affluent Jadriya neighbourhood, known as the Representation Office of Ansar Allah. It is headed by Abu Idris al-Sharafi, a prominent Houthi representative with ties to Iraq dating back to 2016.
According to the Iraqi official, the government has designated residences for members of the Houthi representation and required them to provide advance information about their movements within Baghdad and other provinces.
The official added that the group’s members had been informed of the decision several days earlier.
The directive explicitly prohibits activities conducted from Iraqi territory against Saudi Arabia or other countries in the region, citing the principles of good neighbourliness and non-interference in the affairs of other states enshrined in the Iraqi constitution.
Houthi leaders have reportedly made several visits in recent months to political officials, as well as commanders from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and other armed factions in Baghdad and several provinces. Iraq is home to numerous Iran-backed armed groups.
The Iraqi official said members of the Houthi group could no longer organise political or media activities relating to the ongoing war in Yemen.
The restrictions come about a week after al-Zaidi visited Saudi Arabia and met Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, holding talks on security, political and economic issues.
During the meeting, al-Zaidi assured the crown prince that Iraq would not allow its territory to be used to launch attacks against Saudi Arabia or other countries in the region, the Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.
“Iraq’s firm position is not to allow its territory to be used as a launching pad for any attacks or actions that affect the security of the kingdom and the countries of the region, and to be keen on adhering to the principles of good neighbourliness and respecting the sovereignty of Iraq and brotherly and friendly countries,” al-Zaidi’s office said in a statement cited by INA.
During the Houthis’ lightning offensive in Yemen last month, Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was struck by drones - forcing Riyadh to temporarily suspend operations along the export route, which Saudi Arabia uses as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia said the drones originated in Iraq.
Baghdad conducted its own investigation and concluded that the strikes had been launched from Iraqi territory, although no group claimed responsibility.
Speaking to TNA, retired Iraqi Army Colonel Saad al-Jughaifi said the latest restrictions on Houthi representatives were consistent with international pressure to curb support for groups Washington describes as Iran’s regional proxies.
Al-Jughaifi also disclosed that measures introduced several months ago had restricted prominent members of Lebanon’s Hezbollah armed group and the Houthi movement from accessing Iraq’s financial transfer system, including banks, currency exchange and remittance companies.
He said restrictions had also affected their access to Iraqi Airways.
Al-Jughaifi added that the measures were intended to prevent Iraq from facing further financial, economic and political crises resulting from an adverse international classification.
He said that the Houthis had been hosted in Iraq under the government of Adel Abdul Mahdi in 2018, but their presence had since expanded in terms of personnel, headquarters and offices. Some members had also brought their families to live in Iraq.
Yemen’s civil war, in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015, reignited in September following the collapse of a years-long truce.
The Houthis have tried to impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, targeting its tankers and seizing large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, a key route for oil exports.
The conflict has also driven up energy prices, with the Houthis launching repeated missile attacks against the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has been targeted 20 times since the beginning of the month, with a recent attack killing 13 people and injuring more than 300.

articles.title: Blame Russia, ignore the money? Israel’s election interference debate
articles.body:
Blame Russia, ignore the money? Israel’s election interference debate
As Israel prepares for the October 27 elections, accusations of foreign interference are intensifying. While Israeli leaders have pointed to Iran, Russia, and China, journalist Nick Kolyohin argues that greater scrutiny should be directed at Western funding of Israeli media outlets and civil society organizations, which he believes may be influencing the country’s political discourse.
With election day approaching, political parties are stepping up efforts to attract voters and consolidate their support.
The right-wing camp, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is seeking to rally hawkish voters behind him, potentially at the expense of other conservative parties. The opposition bloc is trying to persuade voters to abandon Netanyahu and shift their support to its side.
Yet the battle for the Israeli electorate is not being fought exclusively within the country’s borders. Foreign actors are also seeking to shape the political landscape and influence the outcome of the election.
Foreign meddling
Several days ago, speaking to Channel 14, Netanyahu raised this concern.
“Iran is trying to damage the elections with the help of its terror arms Hamas and Hezbollah. It is totally true – they say it openly that they need to topple me because their real desire is to destroy the State of Israel.”
Iran, however, is not the only country accused of interference. In July, speaking at the Knesset, opposition leader Yair Lapid also accused China and Russia of attempting to meddle.
“The elections are drawing closer. Iran is involved, Russia is involved, and influence operations are running rampant on social media. They want to divide us, strengthen the extremists, weaken the moderates, and sow chaos and hatred.”
Nick Kolyohin, a veteran Israeli journalist and Russia expert, disputes the accusations against Moscow, saying he has seen no evidence of Russian interference in the current or previous election cycles:
“I am not witnessing, neither in the current round, nor in the previous, any influence from the Russian side.”
“I am not even sure which side Russia prefers in this internal dispute between the different political parties. Israeli politicians are not speaking about Russia so it doesn’t even make any sense for Moscow to interfere because it is not clear which government is going to be good or bad for the Kremlin,” he said.
Kolyokhin maintains that the broader relationship between the two countries lends weight to his assessment. Despite periodic setbacks and fluctuations, economic ties and trade have continued. Diplomatic relations and cooperation have also endured through some of the most turbulent periods in recent history, including the Syrian civil war, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, and the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023.
Relations between the countries’ leaders have also largely remained cordial. Although then-Prime Minister Yair Lapid strongly criticized Russia over its actions in Ukraine, relations between Moscow and other Israeli prime ministers, including Naftali Bennett and Netanyahu, have been more amicable.
“I know for a fact, including from my sources within the PM office, that the current premier has very good and close relations with President Vladimir Putin. Israel understands that from time to time Moscow needs to slap it [publicly] because it is a part of a broader geopolitical game but in the end of the day this will not sour the relationship between the nations.”
The West dictates
Kolyohin argues that while Russia has come under scrutiny over alleged interference in the upcoming elections, another potential source of foreign influence is receiving far less attention: liberal political circles in Europe and the US.
“For many years, the European Union and the Democratic Party have been pouring money into the Israeli NGOs, news outlets, journalists, think tanks and experts – all of whom are located on the left side of the Israeli political map. So they ended up promoting European interests, which I find outrageous, especially now, when the EU is openly unfriendly towards Israel.”
In recent years, several European countries have recognized Palestine despite Israeli appeals. European governments have also pursued sanctions on Israeli products manufactured in the West Bank and Golan Heights, imposed embargoes on military equipment, and suspended bilateral agreements.
Kolyohin says he has evidence to support his allegations of Western interference. In recent weeks, he says, he obtained three documents that point to substantial financial transfers from Western liberal circles to Israeli left-wing organizations.
The first transfer involved around $48,000 (€43,000). According to Kolyohin, the money came from Canal France International (CFI), a French public media-development agency, and went to the Seventh Eye, an Israeli liberal outlet known for its critical coverage of Netanyahu.
CFI has also reportedly provided hundreds of thousands of euros to another liberal Israeli organization, the Israeli Association of Internet. While the stated objective was to support Israel and combat disinformation, Kolyohin suspects that the underlying motivations extend beyond those publicly declared goals.
The US State Department has allegedly followed a similar approach. Kolyohin says documents in his possession show that the Institute for Israel’s National Studies, one of Israel’s most reputable think tanks, received more than $500,000 from 2023-2025.
“This is one of the ways for the west to censor and control the information in Israel and in this way they can also interfere in the elections, and promote their agenda among the public.”
According to the journalist, the Western agenda extends beyond the promotion of liberal ideas. He argues that another key objective is to foster anti-Russian sentiment in Israel, a goal he believes is advanced through media outlets and think tanks that receive Western funding.
“These journalists and experts learned fast that if they want to be honored, invited to conferences, and get prizes, they need to criticize Russia even if that is contrary to the interests of Israel itself,” Kolyohin said.
“You have to understand: Russia is an important partner of Israel but very often the Israeli government is trying not to flash these tight relations petrified by what the media and the experts are going to say.”
Witch hunt campaign?
Kolyohin says he has personally experienced what he regards as the consequences of anti-Russian sentiment in Israel. Several Israeli news outlets have investigated his alleged connections to the Kremlin. His name is frequently associated with what local outlets describe as Russian propaganda, and he believes these efforts have damaged his professional standing.
In 2025, he was barred from press conferences held by Israel’s Foreign Ministry after asking Foreign Minister Gideon Saar to comment on Ukraine’s glorification of the Nazis.
A year later, he was removed from a plane carrying Netanyahu to Washington, where the prime minister was scheduled to meet with Trump. According to Kolyohin, the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, wanted to examine his background and ties.
“They are after journalists like me because I am not slamming Russia like the rest of them. They are after me because I dare to speak to the Russian media, I dare to give interviews and do reports. That’s why they want to discredit me, and they are even trying to tilt the PM office and the Shin Bet against me.”
Kolyohin has filed a lawsuit against several Israeli organizations that receive foreign funding and says he is prepared to continue his legal fight to find out the truth: Who funds Israeli NGOs, for what purpose, and how is this money used to shape public opinion?

articles.title: Ukraine has shown heroism, but military aid to it has depleted U.S. weapons stocks – Hegseth
articles.body:
Ukraine has shown heroism, but military aid to it has depleted U.S. weapons stocks – Hegseth
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that support for Ukraine under the Biden administration had depleted American weapons stocks. He did not provide specific data on the scale of the reduction.
U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said that Ukraine had demonstrated heroism in confronting Russian aggression, but that the large-scale military assistance provided to Kyiv under the previous U.S. administration had depleted the United States' weapons stocks, UNN reports.
Details
According to the Pentagon chief, Ukrainian troops made significant efforts to defend their country and received substantial support from international partners, including the United States.
Ukraine made heroic efforts, and significant assistance was provided to it. So significant that under the previous administration, weapons stocks were depleted
The Pentagon spoke about the consequences of military assistance to Ukraine
In his statement, the American secretary linked the reduction in U.S. military reserves to the volume of weapons that Washington transferred to Ukraine during Joe Biden's presidency.
At the same time, Hegseth did not specify which categories of weapons he was referring to or the extent to which the corresponding stocks of the U.S. military had been reduced.
The United States remains an important weapons supplier to Ukraine. In particular, European partners continue to rely on American production when providing Ukrainian troops with the necessary systems and ammunition.
The Pentagon chief's statement is his assessment of the consequences of Washington's previous policy. The minister's quoted remarks contain no specific data that would make it possible to assess the scale of the alleged depletion of U.S. military stocks.

articles.title: US will ‘burn’ like France if Democrats win – Trump (VIDEO)
articles.body:
US will ‘burn’ like France if Democrats win – Trump (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump has claimed that America could face similar chaos to the violent unrest sweeping France if the Democrats win next month’s midterm elections, accusing left-wing politicians of fueling mass migration and instability across the West.
France has struggled to contain escalating riots that erupted last month over teacher shortages and crumbling facilities. The protests have since grown into a broader movement against inequality and soaring living costs.
Hundreds of thousands took to the streets over the weekend as demonstrations descended into clashes with police, arson, and looting. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested, hundreds of businesses looted, and buildings torched across the country, while around 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured.
Footage drew comparisons to “scenes from a civil war,” with videos also showing some protesters waving Palestinian flags alongside the French tricolor.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump warned that “Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon,” blaming France’s immigration policies for the unrest.
Trump: Paris is going to be a Muslim city pretty soon. pic.twitter.com/9S5fx0ppPo
— Acyn (@Acyn) October 19, 2026
He sharpened his criticism in a Truth Social post, describing France as a “once-great nation” being “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground.” Trump blamed “migrants, jihadists and communists” for the violence, accused European leaders of surrendering their countries to people unwilling to assimilate and urged them to “close their borders” before it is too late.
Trump then turned the unrest into a pitch for Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterms, warning that scenes of “burning steeples and raging fires” were “what the Radical Dumocrats want to do to AMERICA.” He accused Democrats of embracing radical left-wing ideology and cast the election as a fight for America’s “culture,” “civilization” and “heritage.”
“If you want to see what is at stake in this Election, just look at what is happening in France… Globalist Leftwing Politicians have treasonously imported millions of Third World Migrants who are totally incompatible with Western Values, and despise everything that makes France great... they have surrendered their country to vandals,” he wrote.
Trump’s renewed focus on immigration – a cornerstone of his successful 2024 campaign – comes as his approval ratings slide and Republicans face mounting pressure ahead of the midterms. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday put his approval at 31% – down one point from two weeks earlier and the lowest of either presidential term. Democrats led Republicans 47% to 35% among registered voters on a hypothetical congressional ballot.
Trump repeated his Truth Social message at a Kansas rally for Republican Senator Roger Marshall, whose once-safe seat, according to polls, is now facing a competitive challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor campaigning against the president’s “erratic leadership.” Trump won Kansas by 16 points in 2024, and the state has not elected a Democratic senator in 94 years.

🔸 Donald Trump s’en prend violemment à la France, qu’il décrit comme une « grande nation d’autrefois » en train d’être « conquise, pillée et incendiée » par des « migrants, des djihadistes et des communistes » qui, selon lui, « haïssent le…
— Little Think Tank (@L_ThinkTank) October 20, 2026
The rally kicked off a six-day campaign blitz through Republican strongholds, with stops planned in the Carolinas, Florida, Iowa and Georgia, as Trump seeks to boost turnout and defend the party’s narrow congressional majorities. Democrats need to flip four seats in each chamber to overturn Republicans’ 218-214 House majority and 53-47 Senate advantage.
Trump’s bet on Russian diesel
Trump has also sought to shore up Republican support ahead of the midterms by tackling soaring fuel prices, as the Iran war and tariffs squeeze household budgets. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 68% of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy, including 37% of Republicans.
To ease the pressure, Trump moved to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, blaming fuel shortages on Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure rather than the Iran war and the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The deal with Moscow would release over 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, another 500,000 tons in November and one million tons thereafter. Russian presidential aide Kirill Dmitriev told RT the agreement had an immediate “positive effect,” with New York diesel futures falling 5% on the announcement.
The move, however, drew accusations of “betraying Ukraine” from Democrats and some Republicans, who urged Trump to end the Iran war instead. He defended the deal as “the right choice for the American People” and later went further by invoking a national-interest exemption to suspend recently enacted Russia sanctions, including 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

articles.title: South Korea recalls some diplomatic staff from Ukraine over POW dispute
articles.body:
South Korea recalls some diplomatic staff from Ukraine over POW dispute
South Korea has decided to recall some of its diplomatic staff from Ukraine due to what Seoul considers a lack of positive steps by Kyiv to resolve a dispute over the public disclosure of information regarding the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war, as well as the ongoing risk of Russian airstrikes.
Source: Yonhap, a South Korean news agency, citing Park Doo-soon, spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of South Korea
Details: Park Doo-soon said at a regular press briefing that Ukraine has yet to take "positive steps" to resolve the diplomatic dispute regarding Kyiv's unilateral disclosure of the news that two North Korean POWs had been transferred to Seoul, and that persistent threats of airstrikes make it difficult to ensure the safety of diplomatic personnel.
Despite this partial recall, the spokesperson noted that South Korea will maintain the necessary diplomatic contact with Ukraine led by a chargé d'affaires ad interim, adding that all consular staff will remain in the country to continue efforts to protect South Korean citizens.
Earlier in October, South Korea recalled its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, as Seoul expressed regret over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's public disclosure of the transfer of the North Korean prisoners of war.
Seoul is demanding an official explanation and an apology from Ukraine regarding Zelenskyy's disclosure of the information. However, the Office of the President of Ukraine has denied that there was any agreement to maintain confidentiality on the matter.
Background:
- South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said Ukraine had breached a non-disclosure agreement by publicly revealing the transfer of the two North Korean POWs to South Korea and that making the information public could lead to numerous problems.
- Zelenskyy's communications adviser, Dmytro Lytvyn, denied that Ukraine had breached any non-disclosure agreement with South Korea.
- However, the South Korean president's office demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine for disclosing the transfer.
